ECHO OF THE PAST
Aug 9th 1955 PAR 51030-1 (PNR-G)

ECHO OF THE PAST
Massive work horses bend to the
traces and the gleaming barley
falls before the binder to bring
an 'Old Master' touch to the harvest
scene on Mr. J.L. Cornish's farm at
East Charleton, near Kingsbridge,
Devon.
East Charleton Farm is the last
stronghold of heavy draught horses
in this area. Tractors and combine
harvesters, as in most other parts of
Britain, have taken their place.
In any event, there are few men
nowadays, who could be found to manage
a three-horse team on a binder.

PRESS PREVIEW OF NEW "PACKAGE DEAL" HOMES.
THE LIVING ROOM - UPSTAIRS....

			A press view was held this afternoon
at Canterbury of the new "Package Deal" homes -
built by JONMIL Building Developments.. The houses
have precast plastic roofs - central heating
throughout; fitted furnishings - integral garage..
The idea is for the purchaser to walk into the
house - which is ready to occupy.. It is priced
at between £2,000 to £3,850 exluding land.. The
bedrooms are downstairs. The builders cope with
everything - purchasing land - mortgage etc.. for
the purchaser.

KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:- 	The Living room - which is
upstairs - seen from the dining recess - showing
the unusually shaped roof which is made of fibre
glass.. This house is priced at £1,500 excluding
land.
			JSS/KEYSTONE 	RC/722539.

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION TUESDAY'S EVENINGS 2.7.46.

BRITAIN'S ROLLERS MAKE THE ROADS OF THE WORLD.
July 1946
Britain has long been famous in the production of road
rollers and other types of road construction machinery,
and the "Invicta" horse of the products of Messrs Aveling-
Barford of Grantham is to be seen even in the most out
of the way spots of the globe. The latest order received
by this firm is for a million pounds worth of road rollers
destined for use in all parts of India. Besides this huge
order, they have others in hand worth threefold for the
supply of machinery to all parts - from Iceland in the
north to New Zealand in the south, and only lack of labour
and further supplies of raw materials prevents the accept-
ance of additional contracts. This work has not been gained
by sitting at home - their representatives have travelled
the world and the result of their missions is seen today in
the increased activity in the Grantham factory, as illustrated
by the accompanying pictures : -

Front rollers of "GD" ten-ton roller being packed
ready for export.
File Industries Road Maintenance Machinery x Filed Rollers

23. 1. 56.

MAKING NEW RIGGING FOR NELSON'S FLAGSHIP "VICTORY"

A team of men and women have started work at Chatham
to make a complete new rigging for Nelson's Flagship,
"VICTORY". They are working in the same timber-built
rope "walks" used by the men who refitted Victory for
Trafalgar after she had been five years in the Medway
as a prison hospital ship. The work is being carried
out at Chatham's Ropery - the Admiralty's only rope-
making establishment. Methods of making the rope are
almost the same as in the days of Nelson, except that
women are employed in some of the operations, now done
by machines.

te.text:
MAKING BASKETS FOR THE FRUIT SEASON.  E. M./MAE.

There is a big demand for fruit baskets from the orchard
districts at this time and Severnside basket makers are
working long hours to try and meet it.  Foreign competition
has, of recent years, had a discouraging effect on the basket-
making trade which, in this district, has been carried on as
a family art throughout the years.  The withies from which
the baskets are made grow on the banks of the river and after
two or three years drying, are boiled in special outdoor
boilers to make them supple.  One of the "pot hampers" as
these fruit baskets are called, takes about one hour and a
half to make and will stand several years rough usage.

Photo shows:- Mr. Venfield, who is carrying on the work of
his father, making "Pot hampers".

te.text:
LN 294440         DAW         LONDON BUREAU
LONDON'S NEW SKYSCRAPERS
LONDON :  PHOTO SHOWS :-  A NEW ELEVEN-STORY BLOCK OF
FLATS ON THE EDGE OF WIBLEDON COMMON, LONDON.
PLANET NEWS FEATURE SERVICE 1955       PN-N

LN 294440 - 294443    DAW         LONDON BUREAU
LONDON'S NEW SKYSCRAPERS
LONDON :  LONDONERS ARE GRADUALLY LEARNING HOW TO SCRAPE
SKIES AND LIKE IT. BLOCKS OF FLATS 10, 12 AND EVEN 14
STORIS HIGH ARE RISING ON THE EDGES OF RICHMOND PARK,
PUTNEY HEATH, WIMBLEDON COMMON AND WANDSWORTH COMMON.
SOME ARE ALREADY FINISHED AND THE TENANTS HAVE MOVED IN.
THERE NEW HOMES ARE A STRIKING AND IMPRESSIVE SIGHT -
EXCEPT TO OLD RESIDENTS WHOSE TWO AND THREE-STORY HOUSES
ARE OVERLOOKED BY THESE TOWERING MINIATURE SKYSCRAPERS.
THE NEW BUILINGS DON'T JUST DISFIGURE THE PLEADANT LANDSCAPE
THAT USED TO BE ON THEIR DOORSTEPS. THEY OBLITERATE IT.
IT IS HARD LUCK ON THE PEOPLE OF ROEHAMPTON AND WIMBLEDON.
BUT LONDONERS MUST LIVE SOMEWHERE. THERE CAN BE NO COMPLAIN
AGAINST THE BUILDINGS THEMSELVES. THEY ARE DESIGNED TO
INCLUDE THE BEST ELEMENTS IN MODERN ARCHITECTURAL STRUCTURE.
THEY ARE BEAUTIFUL EXAMPLES OF STYLE AND INSIDE ARE
COMFORTABLE AND EMINENTLY LIVABLE-IN. AND THE LONDON
COUNTY COUNCIL ARE BUILDING THEM IN SETTINGS ABOUT WHICH
THERE CAN BE NO COMPLAINT. £4,500,000 IS BEING SPENT ON
15 BLOCKS OF THESE FLATS AS PART OF THE ROEHAMPTON
DEVELOPMENT SCHEME, AND MORE FOR HUNDRED-FOOT STRUCTURES IN
OTHER AREAS. IT IS ALSO EXPECTED THAT WHEN THE SLUM
CLEARANCE PROJECTS GET UNDER WAY, THESE SKYSCRAPERS CAN BE
BUILT IN CLEARED AREAS NEARER TO THE HEART OF LONDON, THUS
HELPING TO SOLVE THE URGENT AND CRITICAL REHOUSING PROBLEM
IN AREAS WHERE LAND IS SCARCE.

FIRST OF BRITAIN'S NEW POWER STATIONS READY FOR ROYAL
OPENING.

Kingston, Eng: The first of Britain's 25 new power
stations - the 5 1/4 million sterling project at Kingston-
on-Thames, Surrey - is ready for the official opening
by the King on October 27.
The remainder of the 25 stations are scheduled for
completion by 1952 and will ease Britain's power shortage.
Shortage of labour has, however, created a bottleneck in
the building of the new stations for production of
generating plant has, according to a Ministry of Supply
official, outstripped the building programme.
The machinery is being stored until the stations are ready.

activity: Rescue of five miners from a flooded pit via bucket lift.

te.text:
HERALD REPORTERS     LYDBROOK, Glos., Thursday
FIVE miners, the last of 150 trapped in a flooded pit,
were tonight hoisted 130 yards up an old air shaft
in the Forest of Dean by a hastily-rigged bucket-and-
winch lift.
These five, who had been
"exploring" disused workings
for coal that could be worked,
had fought their way to that
air shaft, through water at
times neck-high, for seven
hours.
The rest of the 150, who were
working in the Arthur and Edward
Pit when the water swept in, were
hauled up the ordinary pit shaft
in the cage.
People from this mining hamlet
cheered the five wildly. Pit de-
puties held a final count, ticking
off the names on a list: Frank
Bradley, Oswald Simmonds, Ernie
Barnfield, Bert Sims, Tom Main-
waring. . .

UP to safety in the bucket-
and-winch lift comes 67-
year-old Bert Sims—one of the
last five of 150 miners who were
trapped in the flooded pit.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

"HOSPITAL" WHERE THEY RE-BOX THE COMPASS. 
 CH/RS 
 In a rural setting, a peer's former home, is one of the least 
 known departments of the Admiralty - the Compass Observatory 
 at Ditton Park, near Slough, Bucks, where nearly 100 delicately 
 fingered work-people may be found industriously pulling compasses 
 to pieces and rebuilding them. This department saves the 
 nation many thousands of pounds a year for it is here that the 
 gyro and magnetic compasses of the Navy and Air Force are 
 assembled, reconditioned and tested. Between three and four 
 thousand R.A.F. compasses are handled a year and several hundred 
 Naval ones. It is only on rare occasions that a new compass 
 is purchased. 
 Photo shows - 'Rough seas to order'. Testing gyro compasses 
 for rolling error at the Admiralty Compass Observatory. Note 
 the compasses are being swung to simulate the rolling of a ship.

te.text:
XH)           KENT HOP STRINGING COMPETITION

Believed to be the only contest of its kind in the world
the annual hop stringing competition, organised by The
Weald of Kent Ploughing Match Association, took place
to-day at Spitzbrook, Collier Street, Kent.  About 40
Kentish farmworkers, all experts in hop stringing, and
many of them coming from families which have worked in
the hop gardens for generations, took part.  The
stringer's job is to prepare hop gardens for the next
crop by putting up a complicated pattern of strings
which the hops can climb.  He works with a pole 10 feet
long, guiding the string (drawn from a bag slung over
his shoulder) from hooks in the ground to others hanging
on wires overhead.      He is followed by a "bander in"
(usually female) who binds together the groups of
vertical strings comprising a "hill."  In the
competition, each stringer completes a "cant" of 200
hills.  Some 40 miles of string are used in the
process.  Competitors score points for speed, neatness
and economy in the use of string.  The object of the
competition is to stimulate interest in the craft and
to encourage ability in a highly skilled branch of
agricultural work.

Photo shows:-  Miss A. Hewitt banding in for Mr. B.
King during the competition.

X File - Aviation - Post War "Bristol Brabazon"
FILE INDUSTRY

THE BRISTOL TYPE 167 LOW-WING CANTILEVER MONOPLANE -
SOMETIMES UNOFFICIALLY REFERRED TO AS THE BRABAZON I.

Picture shows:- the Zeppelin-like fuselage of the
giant plane under construction at the Bristol
Aeroplane Company's works at Bristol.
S/P
SUPPLIED L.N.A.
V. 39798

BRITAIN'S BIGGEST LAND PLANE.

The BRISTOL TYPE 167 low wing cantilever monoplane,
sometimes unofficially referred to as the BRABAZON I,
is the biggest land plane yet to be built by the
British aircraft industry and is now taking shape in the
Bristol Aeroplane Company's factory at Filton, Bristol.
Estimated to cost £4,000,000 the 167 is being
built solely for flight development work and is expected
to fly in the early summer of 1947.
The aircraft with an all up weight of 285,000 lbs,
- approximately 126 tons - will have a maximum level
speed of more than 300 m.p.h. at 25,000 feet, a cruising
speed of 250 m.p.h., at 25,000 feet, and a still air
range of 5,000 miles.

Please return to
ART LIBRARY DAILIES OF

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY 23RD SEPTEMBER 1964

TWO SLIPWAYS NEEDED TO BUILD BRITAIN'S
BIGGEST TANKER EVER.
G. 9633 SEPTEMBER 1964.
ERF.
THE CONSTRUCTION OF BRITAIN'S FIRST 100,000-TON
TANKER, WHICH IS BEING BUILT FOR BRITISH PETROLEUM,
IS NOW WELL UNDER WAY, AND SHE IS DUE TO BE LAUNCHED
FROM THE VICKERS-ARMSTRONGS YARD AT BARROW-IN-FURNESS
EARLY NEXT YEAR.
THE NEW SHIP IS THE FIRST OF TWO
100,000-TONS DEADWEIGHT TANKERS BEING BUILT FOR
BP. TANKER COMPANY - THE SECOND IS UNDER CONSTRUCTION
AT SWAN HUNTER AND WIGHAM RICHARDSON'S YARD ON THE TYNE.
BP'S NEW 100,000-TON TANKER WILL BE 180 FEET IN BREADTH
917'-6" FEET OVERALL IN LENGTH AND HAVE A SUMMER DRAUGHT
OF 49 FEET. ALL THE MACHINERY WILL BE INSTALLED COMPLETE
PRIOR TO LAUNCHING AND IT WILL BE THE GREATEST-EVER
LAUNCHING WEIGHT AT BARROW. AFTER LAUNCHING, ONLY
A FEW WEEKS WILL BE REQUIRED TO PREPARE THE NEW TANKER
FOR FINAL TRIALS.
IN ORDER TO ACCOMMODATE THE GREATER WIDTH
OF THE NEW VESSEL, TWO EXISTING BERTHS, EACH CAPABLE
OF BUILDING VESSELS 100 FEET WIDE, HAVE BEEN REBUILT
INTO A BERTH WHICH CAN TAKE VESSELS 150 FEET IN WIDTH.
PHOTO SHOWS:
BRITAIN'S FIRST 100,000-TON TANKER
UNDER CONSTRUCTION IN THE VICKERS-ARMSTRONGS YARD
FROM WHERE IT WILL BE LAUNCHED EARLY NEXT YEAR.

activity: Customs official boarding and on deck of an arrested French trawler.

te.text:
SIGHTING a French trawler, Notre Dame de Lourdes, within the three-mile limit off Rye Bay, early yesterday, the British gun-boat Kingfisher went alongside. The trawler moved off and Kingfisher followed her for 20 minutes, calling on her to stop.
Then, as she took no notice, the gun-boat fired a round of blank over her bows. The trawler came to a standstill, and later in the day her master was fined £10, including costs, at Dover, for being within British fishery limits.
The master, John Baptiste Margolle, blamed the flood tide for his being within the limit. All his gear was aboard.
There was no suggestion, said the Kingfisher's commander, that the trawl was down.
Top picture shows a customs official on the deck of the trawler in Dover Harbour; below, the officer is seen boarding the vessel from a customs launch. The gun-boat Kingfisher is in the background.

activity: volunteer workers wearing Army capes standing by helpless as rain beats down on the wheat harvest

te.text:
THE TRAGEDY OF BRITAIN'S HARVEST.
FARMERS FIGHT THE WEATHER.         AW/RS

The abnormal rainfall this summer and the absence of a
period of sunny weather to ripen and dry the wheat is
giving the farmers an anxious time - especially now, harvest
time. These pictures, taken today on a farm at Godstone,
Surrey, illustrate just how the weather is interfering
with the harvest. The workers also are losing financially -
they are all volunteers from a harvest holiday camp, and
only get paid when actually working.

Photo shows:-   A picture that tells the story of the [struck through: fight]
struggle to garner the badly needed harvest. Volunteer
workers, wearing the Army capes provided for them, stand
by helpless as the rain further beats down the crops.
Fox August 20th. 46.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

Standing by helpless while
rain ruins the crops, these
cape-clad harvesters were
photographed at Godstone,
Surrey. They had been
forced to abandon work
when rain caused the sheaves
to stick in the cutting
machines.

activity: samples being stored in a cold room at a radio-biological laboratory pending analysis

te.text:
AGRICULTURAL RESEARCH LABORATORY	PC/FRES.

The Agricultural Research Council Radio-biological
Laboratories, near Wantage, Berkshire, is the organisation
that carries out regular tests on milk collected from
milk sampling zones and depots in Great Britain, that
determine the amount of iodine 131 content. The fear
that the quantity of radio active content in milk may
rise because of the recent Russian Nuclear tests is
officially over, and it has been announced in the House
of Lord's by the Minister of Science, Lord Hailsham, that
milk throughout the country is free from a dangerous
level of iodine 131 and is safe for young children.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:- The laboratories cold room where
samples are stored pending final bulking and analysis.
FOX PHOTOS 27TH. NOVEMBER 1961. (2). 655895.

COPYRIGHT SUPPLIED BY
FOX PHOTOS LTD
69/71 FARRINGDON ROAD, LONDON E.C.1

te.text: Industry- Railways - loco + rolling stock const .

XH )             ARMS WORKS TO AID TRANSPORT

Ordnance factories are now switching over one part of
their factory space to peace-time production that will
eventually benefit road and civil transport. The Royal
Gun and Carriage Factory at Woolwich Arsenal (London),
which, during the war, manufactured anything from minute
fuse mechanisms to 16-inch naval guns, is now repairing
hundreds of wooden railway wagons for railway companies
and private owners, as well as an unlimited number of
ex-army trucks for the distressed countries of Europe.

Photo shows:- Workmen busy repairing railway wagons,
while men clear the last war-time ammunition boxes and
gun-barrel cases from the shed - a scene at Woolwich Arsenal.

3/1/46.           (Topical Press)            (Y.21307)

activity: Kenneth Foster, a pipe inspector, examining North Sea gas pipes rusting in a depot at Great Yarmouth.

te.text: Ind - Fuel - Oil from Sea Bed - N. Sea Exps.

DESPITE claims by the tobaccon-
ists, who admittedly were thinking
of something rather different when
they elected actor Andrew Cruick-
shank as Pipeman of the Year last
month, Mr. Kenneth Foster must
be considered a strong contender
for the title.
Mr. Foster is a pipe inspector. As
may be deduced, he inspects pipes. But
the pipes he expertly studies are very
special pipes indeed—35 miles of them,
all intended to carry gas, or oil, from
the North Sea to Britain.
They have to be inspected because
at the moment, all these pipes are
steadily rusting away in a depot at
Great Yarmouth, Norfolk. It is a
process which is likely to continue for
some time—for the time, in fact, it
takes barristers, businessmen, preserv-
ationists and all to argue whether they
should be used to convey gas, or oil, to
a processing plant at Bacton, Norfolk.
A public inquiry begins today and
its machinations will take some time.
Depot officials are fatalistic: 'It
doesn't matter how long they rust
away. We can always brush them up.
And we know they'll be used some-
where.'
In the meantime, Mr. Foster carries
on inspecting. It won't be his fault if
the first North Sea gas (or oil)
pipeline springs a leak.

Kenneth Foster

title: A photographic print of Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip, Visit to Shetlands, August, 1960

activity: Royal visit to the Shetland Islands including a reception in Lerwick.

te.text:
ART LIBRARY
TO
PLEASE RETURN
11 AUG 1960
DAILY HERALD
PROPERTY OF

Shetlanders forgive the Queen
THE roar that greeted the Queen as
she stepped ashore in the Shetland
Islands yesterday told her: "All is for-
given."
Remember the bitter disappointment in
the Shetlands last summer when the
Queen's first-ever visit was cancelled on the
eve of her arrival? The baby was expected.
But the Shetlanders, whose hardy
womenfolk return to the fields 48 hours
after having their babies, are not people to
harbour a grievance.
"Thank you for such a forgiving wel-
come," said the Queen. She, too, remem-
bered the local criticism of her advisers
who were considered "too off-handed."
This was the first visit of a monarch to
the Shetlands since the Viking kings landed
700 years ago.
After the reception in Lerwick, the Queen
in flowerpot hat and loose coat of cyclamen
pink, faced a gale to meet the crofters and
fishermen in their lonely homes strung out
across Shetland.
Joking with the Lerwick lifeboat crew,
Prince Philip was told of their various
"landlubber" trades. He jibed: "I would
not like to go to sea with you lot."
But later he noticed a scroll for valour
on the wall. Every man of that crew had
an award for rescuing a Russian crew in
a midnight gale.
"I take it all back," said Philip.

activity: Theft of a prefab bungalow house in Croydon.

te.text:
DAILY HERALD March 20 1959 5
Stolen—
a house
and all
mod. con.
Herald Reporter
FOUR cheerful young men took a pre-fab bungalow to pieces, loaded it in to a lorry, and drove away.
And that led to the strangest entry that police at Croydon, Surrey, have ever put in their log-book. It reads:
"Stolen; one prefab, with two bedrooms, lounge, kitchen and bathroom, fitted cupboards and all mod. con."
The prefab is — or WAS — in Firtree - avenue, Shrublands, Croydon. It was empty, and had been sold by Croydon council to a man in Suffolk, who was expected to take it away.
But the four young men beat him to it.
'A ROW'
As they worked, unhurriedly, neighbours watched, thinking they were contractors' men.
Mr. Charles Jones, a plasterer, who lives in the next house, said yesterday: "I was an innocent witness to the crime. I had a row with one of the men for flinging bits and pieces into my garden."
Police admit they haven't a clue — not even a finger-print.

activity: Mrs Carol Hammond and her children Gary, Ian and Neal in their 9th floor flat, which they are frequently unable to leave due to broken lifts.

te.text:
ARTHUR STEEL            22.2.66
LIFT TROUBLE IN COUNCIL FLATS
When the lifts in the huge blocks of flats are out of order(and this
oftens happen) old people and mothers with babies are trapped in their
flats as the stairs are unmanageable.
OPS...Mrs Carol Hammond and her children Gary 7, Ian 2 and Neal
10 months are often sealed off in their 9th floor flat in James
Hammett House, Bethnal Green.E.

TWICE a week, and sometimes
more, the world becomes a for-
bidden place for Carol Hammond
and her children. Inaccessible. Un-
attainable. Out of bounds.
Man may send Lunikular things
up to the moon, but the family
cannot even get down to ground
level. And if they could, they
wouldn't get up again.
So they stay put, trapped in their
ninth-floor home—the victims of lifts
which work if you're lucky but don't if
you're not.
The Hammonds are just one of the
families who suffer from liftlessness in
the Dorset Estate flats at Tower
Hamlets, London.
ONE-HOUR CLIMB
There's the woman of 76 who lives on
the 10th floor and needs support when
she walks.
When the lifts give up—"and some-
times they don't get fixed for days"—
her 74-year-old brother climbs up and
down the stairs to go shopping for her.
There's 58-year-old Albert Yeomans
who has asthma and lives on the
eighth floor. Once he took an hour to
climb the stairs.
So now, when he gets home and finds
the lift motionless he goes to his son's
home and sleeps there. Anything but
face those stairs.
Then there's Mrs. Ham-
mond, 28-year-old mother of
three young sons—Garry,
aged seven, Ian, who is two,
and 10-month-old Neal.
She says: "Whenever I want
to take the children out in the
pram I send Garry to make sure
the lift is working.
"If it isn't, I just give up
and stay home. This has hap-
pened too often to count."
The borough council are "dis-
tressed" about the situation.
New lifts have been ordered but
they are not expected for an-
other five months.
The borough's housing officer,
Miss Joan Simpson, said yester-
day: "The lifts do have a
harder life than those in blocks
of offices and luxury flats, be-
cause children tend to play
around with them.
"Tradesmen probably give
them a hard time, too, by jam-
ming the doors open while they
make deliveries. And perhaps
the lifts are simply getting old."

problem of the cigarette short-
age might be solved.
"I have found out for myself
that many of the heaviest
cigarette smokers are women.
Why is this? In many cases it
is because women either dare
not or cannot smoke a pipe.
"Take, for instance, a woman
who dares not smoke a pipe in
public because she feels em-
barrassed. That woman can
only go on smoking her 20 or
30 cigarettes a day.
"Now if ladies' pipes were
designed to look attractive and
dainty, then I believe women
would go as crazy about them
as they did about slacks, which
really came from the men's
trousers."
When told of the idea, a
famous London firm of pipe-
makers said that they already
have a number of pipes at all
prices specially designed for
women (the one you see below
has a ring of diamonds set in
platinum round the stem, and
costs £9 10s.). Three or four
a week are sold.
Manager of another firm said
that he didn't think women
would go to the bother of fill-
ing and cleaning a pipe.
What do women smokers
think?

She's in the dairy business.
THINK of 75 doorsteps in
a row and a pint of milk
put on each every morning
for a year.

Butterfly has been doing to win
back her lost record.

give eight gallons of milk to end
a 305-day test period.

the British dairy shorthorn
record—and go on in an attempt
to beat her own world record of
3,390 gallons in 497 days.
Two years ago, Butterfly—
Clanville Lady Butterfly VIII—
set up a new British record by
filling 20,640 pint bottles in 305
days (the cow's year). But a
rival filled 21,360 bottles the next
year.

Weston, said yesterday: "But-
terfly has been giving eight
gallons a day, rising to 11 1/2 gal-

she will have regained the record
with 100 gallons to spare.

of steel the 43 years old 'B' furnace ends
its career.

at the Rotherham works of Steel, Peech and

British total steel output, which are being
replaced by six 100 ton electric arc furnaces
which will produce steel quicker and cheaper.

First hand Arthur Garrison, second hand

as the hundred tons of molten metal in the

te.text:
MOBILE POWER UNIT FOR VENEZUELAN OILFIELDS

A complete electrical sub-station on wheels -
the first of its kind to be constructed in this
country - is now on its way to Venezuela for use
in Shell's oilfields around Lake Maracaibo.  Being
easily mobile at short notice the sub-station will
augment or temporarily replace any of the existing
14 static sub-stations and can also be used to
provide a temporary supply to parts of the oilfields
not served by permanent stations.  The plant and
all necessary control gear are fixed and cabled up
on a towed 40-ton trailer, with accessories carried
in an accompanying truck.  The unit was constructed
by Messrs. Parolle Electrical Plant Co. Ltd. of
Newcastle-upon-Tyne.

PICTURE SHOWS:- View of the mobile electrical sub-
station on its trailer.

activity: R. Weeks competing in a hop stringing competition at Pattenden Farm.

te.text:
APRIL 9th. 1968.

HOP STRINGING COMPETITION.

          Hop stringers, the name given to men and women
who every year weave the vast "spider's web" of cord
yarn - some 300,000 miles of it - on which will grow
the hops required to flavour the nine thousand million-
odd pints of beer Britons can be expected to drink next
year, had their own competition in Kent today - the
Weald of Kent Ploughing Match Association's annual hop-
stringing competition - held at Pattenden Farm, Marden,
Kent.     The stringers carry the yarn in baskets slung
over their shoulders, and by means of poles, ten feet or
more long and tipped with iron tubing through which the
cord runs, thread it from pegs in the ground to hooks set
on wires 15 1/2 feet above the gardens.    The result is that
from each site of a growing hop plant, called "a hill",
arises a pattern of string resembling the spokes of an
umbrella - the name given to the type of stringing most
frequently met with in the South East.   The stringers,
who in the competition have to "string a cant of about
200 hills", are followed by assistants - usually women -
who act as "banders-in" and tie each group of four vertical
strings together about five feet from the ground.

KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:-      MR. R. WEEKS, a competitor
          in the open class, displays his art at "stringing"
          during the competition today.
                    H/keystone       ML/A807909

te.text:
STEPHENS/CARDIFF.              D.H.                2.12.56
THERE'S COAL IN THEM THAR WOODS.
In the Forest of Dean, Gloucestershire, there are
several large coal mines, and also small private levels,
worked by handfuls of men.
One of these is the Edge End Colliery, near Coleford,
where five men work.     One of these miners is Ted
Horrobin, who has spent many years underground.   But
now he drives the haulage engine at the top of the
colliery level, and cuts and shapes pit props in the
forest clearing outside the level.    Running past there
is the main Monmouth-Gloucester road, and probably
most of the people who pass think that Ted is a forestry
worker.   But the wood that he cuts so skilfully is 
nearly all imported.
OPS.   Ted Horrobin chatting with one of his friends,
75-years-old Ted Baldwin, who spent 53 years working in
the Forest minexs.    With Mr. Baldwin is his dog Spot.

activity: Bakers and Master Bakers judging bread at a baking competition at Caxton Hall.

te.text:
By BARBARA MATTHEWS
IT WAS a magnificent bloomer, with a beautifully symmetrical crust and a crum that surpassed them all for its sheen, its even holes, its bluish tint and its superb aromatic flavour.
And it won the British Baker silver challenge shield, the bakery trade's most important trophy, at the Caxton Hall in London yesterday.
Mr. Sidney Geary, of Valley Bakeries, Ratby, Leics, carried off the shield on behalf of his son and partner, Charles, who actually baked the loaf.
Competition was fierce amongst different shaped loaves - bloomers, tins, farmhouses - and, in other categories of the contest, between hand-raised pork pies, Easter cakes with flop-eared bunnies, and scenes from Swan Lake, painted in confectioners' colours.
A loaf may seem a simple object beside these, but its judging was a complex ritual of prodding, stroking and sniffing (or, as bakers put it, testing the aromatic flavour).
Judges were looking for the sheen, the bluish tint a correctly-fermented loaf should possess, and the holes that prove there was still life in the dough.
"That is the way to make a loaf properly white," Mr. Geary told me. "Not bleaching the flour."
Mr. Geary's firm, three generations of bakers who supply about 150 Leicester shops, is what the trade considers a "small" baker. "We make our bread the old-fashioned way, although with modern equipment," he said.
"This loaf was baked on the oven bottom, and we managed to bring the dough to the peak of fermentation. It was a test of skill."

PRINCESS AT A CHRISTENING

Mersham,Kent,Eng; Princess Elizabeth, who is
expecting her second baby this summer, attended a
christening ceremony in the tiny church here as a
godmother. The baby christened, five-weeks old
Michael John Ulick, is the second son of Lord
and Lady Brabourne.
For the Princess, it was her second visit to Mersham
since her wedding. Last summer she watched her
husband play for the local team in a cricket match.
The new baby's three-year-old brother, Norton,
Louis Philip Knatchbull, has the Duke of Edinburgh
as a godfather.

she attended the chistening of Lord and Lady
Brabourne's child, five-weeks old Michael, at Mersham
church.

te.text:
MANUFACTURING THE "FULLY FASHIONED".
NYLON HOSE IN THE MAKING.

British womenfolk are eagerly awaiting the
arrival in the shops of the supplies of Nylon hose -
items to bring a little luxury to the austerity ridden
legs of Britain. Stocking manufacturers throughout the
country are experimenting, calculating costs and planning
to produce sufficient quantities of stockings made of this
all wonderful, but mysterious material known as 'Nylon'.
Eventually Nylon stockings will be remarkably cheaply
produced, but initially it is expected that they will cost
about 15/- a pair, for 'fully fashioned' and about 8/11
for the 'semi' variety.

KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS: Miss Emily Claxton, is a "looper".
This entails sewing up the soles of the stocking without
leaving a seam. The job needs nine months experience
for real efficiency. Photograph taken at a British
Stocking factory.
GK/HSS  Keystone  FD 3466/12

te.text:
The book cover is made
separately then meets the
book & the two are assembled
in this machine

ROPER                                   16.3.39

50 to 100,000 FULLY BOUND BOOKS PER WEEK.
Some of the largest Perfector printing
machines in Europe:  Printing 64 pages on
each side of the sheet.
The copy from the author goes to Linotype
machines - they have a keyboard similar to
that of a typewriter - which transforms the
printed word into metal type.  The type is
made up into a page form which has a 
facsimile taken off it in paper flong,
from which the metal cast is produced.
Plates are assembled in special order on the
bed of the printing machine and after the
application of ink, the printed sheet is
produced.
The printed sheet goes through nearly half-
a dozen operations such as folding, gathering,
sowing and cutting, when it is transformed
into the bound copy sold to the public.
Real leather is used for the making of cases.
Real 22 carat gold is applied to the lettering.
Someofzsthe
Above is one of the machines used in the
Coplax process.  Its object is to produce
the concave front, and the convex back and
hinge.
OPS.

activity: design and manufacture of pre-cast concrete embrasures for sandbagged blockhouses

te.text:
B EMBRASURES FOR SANDBAGGED BUILT BLOCKHOUSES.
The weak feature in all rapidly constructed blockhouses
is the wooden framing used to form the opening.  The
opening does not protect the rifleman because the rim
can be penetrated by a bullet, also the splintered wood
carried away by the bullet can produce nasty wounds.
The present suggestion is to pre-cast the embrasure
opening of the desired aperture and angle, the outer
extremity having a light sheet steel framing embedded
in the face to prevent the concrete edges shattered by
a bullet from being detached and forming missiles.
The embrasure weighs less than 1½ cwt. and can easily
be lifted into place by two men.   Manufacture can be
made in quite simple wooden moulds by any local building
contractor, breeze block manufacturer, in Corporation
yards, and so on;  using the quick setting concrete
and be produced ready for installation within 24 hours.

discovery was made during blasting operations in connection with
laying sewage pipes at Lester Front. Large pieces of rock were
seen to be encrusted with bright metal. Closer inspection by an
expert revealed that the metal was undoubtedly silver.

NEW BANKNOTE PLANT. MJH/BER.

Rapid progress is being made on the Bank of England's new
printing works at Debden Essex) which is to replace St.
Luke's, Old Street, City. St Luke's at present employs 1200
people and many of these will transfer to Debden, but jobs
will be offered to local people to replace those unable to make

and 10s. banknotes, documents for internal use in the Bank of
England will be printed at the Debden plant which is 
situated on the Debden L.C.C. Estate.

te.text:
BRITISH STAINED GLASS WINDOWS FOR
U.S.A. CHURCH.                               MJH/HT.
An American Church has ordered three 21-foot stained-
glass windows from Britain's oldest firm of glassmakers.
The windows, depicting events from the Apocalypse, have
been commissioned by St. Bernard's Church, Mount Lebanon,
Pennsylvania, from the Whitefriars Studios, of Messrs.
James Powell & Sons, Ltd. Wealdstone (Mddx), who are not only
designing and glazing the windows, but have also made the actual
glass being used in them.  The firm, founded in 1680, is the
only one in Britain to make their own glass, which they do to their
designers' exact requirements, as did the itinerant stained-glass
craftsmen of the Middle Ages.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:       MR. WALTER GILLETT of East Ham (East London)
seen at the Whitefriars Studios, Wealdstone (Mddx) fixing a

inspection.

activity: Men at work erecting locking frames for signal boxes at the G.W. signal works at Reading.

te.text:
READING.

MAKING THE "EYES" OF THE RAILWAY.

Signalling is one of the big items of railway expenditure.
At Reading, for example, the G.W.R. employs hundreds of men
entirely on the upkeep of signals. Here they make everything
for signals, from the huge posts themselves to the electric
coils used in the modern track circuit system. Bells, watches
and lamps are all connected with signals and have to be made
here. Even the signal boxes are made in this universal factory.

Photo shows- Men at work erecting locking frames for signal
boxes at the G.W. signal works at Reading.
Fox Jany 8th. 36.

COPYRIGHT

6, TUDOR STREET,

activity: prototype houses built under the 5M system of construction for Sheffield City Council

te.text:
CROWN COPYRIGHT RESERVED. MINISTRY OF HOUSING & LOCAL GOVERNMENT.
Four prototype houses built for the Sheffield City Council by the
Public Works Department under the 5M system of construction devised
by the Research and Development Group of the Ministry of Housing
and Local Government. This system, which marks a new attempt to
bring the advantages of industrialisation into the field of house-
building, has been derived from the 5M CLASP system used at
Stevenage for a group of old people's flatlets. The new system
is called 5M, because as at Stevenage, it is based upon a planning
grid of 1' 8" (5 x the module of 4"). The object has been to
modify the CLASP system, which has been shown to have advantages in
the reduction of site labour and building time, to suit the
performance standards, and the levels of cost, of 2-storey housing.

Ministry of Housing & Local Government.         January, 1963

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
30 JAN 1963
PLEASE RETURN

activity: Princess Anne launching the tanker Esso Northumbria at Wallsend on the River Tyne.

te.text:
Seconds after the launch the huge bulk of the Esso Northumbria makes the Tyne at Wallsend look like a ditch.
Not bad for a starter
PRINCESS ANNE launched her first ship yesterday with all the aplomb of a veteran.
She pulled a lever, sent a bottle of champagne crashing against the Esso Northumbria's bows, and the monster tanker slid smoothly into the river Tyne.
It was a faultless launch. The quarter-million-ton tanker, the biggest ever built in Britain, did not touch the opposite bank.
The ship made the Tyne at Wallsend look like a ditch. The tanker is 280ft. longer than the QE2, big enough to hide Buckingham Palace behind.
After the bottle-smashing, 40 seconds ticked away before the huge ship, towering above the Princess like a 10-storey building, started to move down the slipway.
As the ship gathered momentum and ploughed into the water, raising clouds of steam and dust, 10,000 people roared their approval.
The £6 1/2 million ship is the first of four ordered by Esso in Britain and was launched on time.
Afterwards Princess Anne, who was presented with a diamond brooch by the shipowners, said: "I have had the honour of launching the largest ship ever built in this country—and for a starter, that is not bad.
"I have experienced the warmth of a Tyneside welcome which has been overwhelming—two things I shall never forget."
Sir John Hunter, chairman of Swan Hunter, yesterday confirmed that the shipyard have won an order for another quarter-million-ton tanker from Anglomar Shipping of London, as reported in yesterday's Sun.
By FRANK DAWES
Shipping Correspondent

PROPERTY
- 3 MAY 1969
Please return to Art Dept.

te.text:
The bungalow at Felpham, near Bognor, which
was raided by police, from which the occupan
escaped.

BOGNOR, Sussex,
Tuesday.
A PRETTY FAIR-HAIRED
YOUNG WOMAN AND
THREE MEN ARE BEING
HUNTED TO-NIGHT BY
SCOTLAND YARD AND THE
POLICE OF ALL THE HOME
COUNTIES.
Hearing that they were living
in a bungalow at Felpham, near
here, and wanting to question
them concerning an epidemic
of burglaries, the police last
night threw a cordon round
their little home.
From their hiding places, the
officers saw, at 2 a.m., one of the men
walking near the bungalow.
They chased him to a car, but were
seconds too late. The car sped off in the
darkness.
The watchers' attention thus diverted,
the woman and the two other men
jumped into another car and made off.
These two cars were both high-powered
saloons.
In a few minutes a police net was
thrown across roads all over Surrey and
Sussex. Messages were flashed to every
police station between the coast and
London.
Level crossings were closed. Cars were
stopped and searched.
But this was not enough to hold the
suspects. At Arundel a car broke
through a police cordon at 70 miles an
hour, and a constable had to jump for
his life.
Near Horsham one car defied three
police challenges.
By now wireless messages had been
sent from Scotland Yard to squad cars
all over the London area giving descrip-
tions of the four people. They were also
circulated by teleprinter to all stations.
One of the suspected cars has been
found abandoned at Arundel, another at
Kingston, after a chase by police along
the by-pass almost into the town.

AERTIST'S IMPRESSION OF THE VAST ANGLO-IRANIAN
SCOTTISH GRANGEMOUTH REFINERY...   28-12-51

Scottish Oils Ltd.. - a member Company
of the Anglo-Iranian Company Group, was formed in 1919
to bring under unified management the Scottish shale-
oil industry which it still controls today.. It owns
twelve shale-pits, four shale retorting works and a
refinery at Pumpherston, Midlothian, where shale-oil
and natural petroleum from Anglo-Iranian's oilfield
at Eakring, Nottinghamshire, are processed.. Grangemouth
Refinery was opened in 1924 with a capacity for
360,000 tons of crude oil a year.. It was temporarily
closed during the war - and work resumed in 1946 - and
has rapidly expanded until it now covers 350 acres and
has a production of 2,250,000 tons per annum..

KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:-  An artists impression made in

te.text:
Industry.. Fuel and Power.. OIL.. From sea bed North Sea
GAS

LN 510490 A.          DAW               LONDON BUREAU
IT'S A GASSER !!!
THE NORTH SEA:              A GIANT YELLOW FLAME
TOWERING 30-40 FEET INTO THE AIR SHOOTS FROM
THE TOP OF THE BRITISH PETROLEUM'S SEA GEM
DRILLING RIG LOCATED 42 MILES EAST OF THE
HUMBER EARLY TODAY.         THE "FLARING" OF THE
WELL NOW FLOWING AT RATE OF TEN MILLION CUBIC
FEET A DAY, MARKS      PROOF OF THE COMMERCIAL
VALUE OF THE BP FIND.  BP HAS BEEN WORKING AT
THE SITE FOR SIX MONTHS -- NOW SEA GEM MOVES
TO A DIFFERENT SITE TWO MILES WEST.  A TOTAL
OF 50 MILLION CUBIC FEET A DAY IS NEEDED FROM
THE WHOLE GAS FIELD TO MAKE THE PROJECT WORTH
WHILE.            7TH DECEMBER 1965 PN-EM
PRESS INTERNATIONAL.

COPYRIGHT
UNITED PRESS INTERNATIONAL (UK) LTD
PLANET NEWS
8. BOUVERIE STREET
LONDON
PHONE:- [illegible]

A GIANT air-sea rescue operation
was in full swing last night after
the 5,600-ton oil-drilling rig, Sea
Gem, with 30 men on her platform, had
collapsed in the icy North Sea.
Flares were dropped by aircraft as an armada
of ships searched the wreckage-strewn sea for
survivors from the ill-fated rig 40 miles off
Grimsby.
Late last night three men were known to be
dead and another seven were missing. Of the 20
known survivors, three are seriously injured.
Two bodies were taken aboard rescue ships. A
third man died in a
helicopter which was
taking him to hospital.
Sea Gem, which was
being used by British
Petroleum to probe the
seabed for gas, capsized
mysteriously yesterday
afternoon.

DID HE FORGET HIS 'ANTI-FREEZE'?
Dec 8th 1956 PAR 60461-2 (PNR-G)

DID HE FORGET HIS 'ANTI-FREEZE'?

Motorists! How are you at 'starting
from cold' (provided you've any petrol)?
Then perhaps you'd like a go at this
icicle-festooned car, which is
expected to start up within 30 seconds
during rigorous pre-production
freezing tests at the Austin Motor
Company's plant at Longbridge, Birmingham.
To make sure the model can stand up to
extremes of cold, it is left to 'soak'
for up to 48 hours in a huge
refrigeration chamber where the
temperature is lowered to 30 degrees below
zero Fahrenheit, 62 degrees of frost.
Technicians who work on the test car
enter the freezing chamber through an
air lock and wear special 'polar'
protective clothing.

te.text:
THEY'RE BAKING BOATS FOR MASS PRODUCTION
February 15th 1958 PAR 69070-2 (Wo-R)

THEY'RE BAKING BOATS FOR MASS PRODUCTION

As sailing fast gains popularity as a sport,
modern mass production methods derived from
those developed during the war for making
wooden aircraft are being applied to the
manufacture of boats at the Hamble, Hampshire,
factory of Fairey Marine Ltd., a subsidiary of
the Fairey Aviation Company.
The craft are 'hot-moulded' from planks of
wooden veneer, a method which eliminates the
old and laborious method of boat-building by
individual craftsmen.
The shell of each boat is composed of layers
of planks applied to a mould to form 'skins'
glued together. Each shell is baked by
steam heat up to 100 degrees Centigrade for
about half an hour. Then it is taken out of
the oven and removed from the mould.
The resulting boat, it is said, will last a
lifetime and is proof against all the normal
ills which affect boats built by other methods.
More than 1,000 boats were produced at Hamble
in 1957, ranging from 7ft. 6in. dinghies to the
26ft. Atalanta sailing cruiser.
Over one-third of the output is exported.
PICTURE SHOWS:- The shell of a 15ft. Albacore
craft being placed in the oven for baking
at Hamble.
February 15th 1958 PAR 69070-2 (Wo-R)

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN EVENING
PAPERS OF MONDAY, FEBRUARY 17th.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
18 FEB 1958

activity: the process of making metal castings from paper flong in book production

te.text:
ROPER               16.3.39

50 to 100,000 FULLY BOUND BOOKS PER WEEK.
Some of the largest Perfector printing
machines in Europe: Printing 64 pages on
each side of the sheet.
The copy from the author goes to Linotype
machines - they have a keyboard similar to
that of a typewriter - which transforms the
printed word into metal type. The type is
made up into a page form which has a
facsimile taken off it in paper flong,
from which the metal cast is produced.
Plates are assembled in special order on the
bed of the printing machine and after the
application of ink, the printed sheet is
produced.
The printed sheet goes through nearly half-
a dozen operations such as folding, gathering,
sewing and cutting, when it is transformed
into the bound copy sold to the public.
Real leather is used for the making of cases.
Real 22 carat gold is applied to the lettering.
[overtyped: Some of the]
Above is one of the machines used in the
Coplax process. Its object is to produce
the concave front, and the convex back and
hinge.
OPS.

activity: drillers of Allerston Forest cheer in triumph after a major natural gas strike on land

te.text:
BRITAIN’S richest strike
of natural gas on land
has been made 6,000ft.
below a Yorkshire forest. A
24-hour test produced 10mil-
lion cubic feet of gas —
enough to supply a large
town.
 “It is a mighty big find,” said
French-Canadian Floyd Des-
rosiers, leader of a team who have
been drilling day and night for
four months.
 He added jubilantly: “We will do
even better when we drill down
another 1,500ft.”
 The drill at Lockton,
near Scarborough, is the
sixth sunk in the area by
Home Oil of Canada, at a
cost of about £100,000.
 Managing director Wil-
liam Ogilvie said: “We
hope we have struck lucky
this time.”
 CAUTION
 And the Gas Council added
to the gusher excitement
yesterday when they an-
nounced that their North Sea
rig Mr. Louie, can produce
12million cubic feet a day.
 Last night there were opti-
mistic hopes that Britain
and the North Sea may be
floating on one gigantic gas
field.
 The full potential of the
Yorkshire well may be
known in about a month.
 Mr. Desrosiers warned:
“Until we sink one or two
more drill holes we shall
have to temper our joy and
enthusiasm with some degree
of caution.”
 But he added confidently:
“There has never been any-
thing like this on land in
Britain. It is its biggest kick
in 25 years’ prospecting.”
LUCKY STRIKE—and the drillers of Allerston Forest cheer in triumph
[Blue felt-tip pen scribbles crossing out text and marking the paper]

the Duke of Edinburgh
yesterday came from this
little boy—who a few weeks

smile at all.

ford, who was the Cinderella of
his family, continually ill-
treated while they lavished love
on his young brother, Peter.
While the parents answered
for their cruelty in court yester-
day, Paul stood outside a coun-
cil home and cheered on the

Games.
Paul's smile shows he has for-
gotten the day when he arrived
at school with a broken arm,
broken nose, bruised leg and
pneumonia. It was for their
responsibility for these that the
parents were jailed.

alloy was inaugurated yesterday at the Redditch (near
Birmingham) works of High Duty Alloys, Ltd., by the

MOBILE POWER UNIT FOR VENEZUELAN OILFIELDS

A complete electrical sub-station on wheels -
the first of its kind to be constructed in this
country - is now on its way to Venezuela for use
in Shell's oilfields around Lake Maracaibo. Being
easily mobile at short notice the sub-station will
augment or temporarily replace any of the existing
14 static sub-stations and can also be used to
provide a temporary supply to parts of the oil-
fields not served by permanent stations. The plant
and all necessary control gear are fixed and
cabled up on a towed 40-ton trailer, with acces-
sories carried in an accompanying truck. The
unit was constructed by Messrs. Parolle Electrical
Plant Co. Ltd. of Newcastle-upon-Tyne.

PICTURE SHOWS:-- The mobile power unit during a
three-hour test carried out in the Newcastle--
upon-Tyne area before dismantling and shipment.

activity: Diamonds in various stages of preparation from rough stones to finished gems, including an emerald cut diamond.

te.text:
LONDON AS WORLD'S GEM INDUSTRY CENTRE?
August, 1945.
Experts who came to England from Holland and Belgium
in 1940, have established in London the business of
manufacture and export of gem diamonds. Exports have
already exceeded a million and a quarter pounds. These
pictures, taken at British Diamond Cutters works in
London, reveal a hive of industry, and there is room
for many more men. British ex-service men included,
to carry on the work. Many of the polishers and cutters
were refugees from Antwerp in 1940, others are ex-service
men who have proved highly skilled after most rapid
tuition. This firm alone exports up to £300,000 worth
of diamonds yearly. The picture shows:-

£12,000 worth of diamonds in various stages of
preparation from rough stones on left to finished
gems on right. In centre is a magnificent emerald
cut diamond worth £2,000. This stone in the rough
weighed 40 carats but cutting and polishing have
reduced it to 14 carats. (No. 6).

COPYRIGHT PHOTO ISSUED BY
CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
INCORPORATING
Central News Illustrations Service,
119, FLEET STREET, LONDON, E.C.4.

te.text:
Helicopt

A NORTH SEA drilling rig was
breaking up yesterday as a
helicopter pilot snatched the
crew of 45 to safety.
The £2 1/4 million rig Ocean Prince
was being battered by waves almost
60ft. high and winds gusting to
90 mph.
Captain Robert Balls carried out
his one-man rescue operation after
the rig's 136ft.-high drilling derrick,
radio room and two cranes had toppled
into the raging sea, and three of its
18 legs had collapsed.
The crew were marshalled at the
undamaged end of the 300ft. by 200ft.
rig to await Captain Balls's helicopter.
As the gale raged on, the Ocean
Prince, moored 110 miles east of Scar-
borough, bumped and bored furiously
against the sea bed. And
last night crewmen esti-
mated that a third of the
rig had fallen into the sea.
Some of the rescued men
were taken to the rig Con-
stellation, 20 miles away,
and some were flown to
land.
Last night a spokesman for
the owners, Burmah Oil Explo-
ration, said the men on Constel-
lation would stay the night
there because of the storm.
Captain Balls, 32-year-old
father of three, was called from
his bed in a Scarborough hotel
at 6am. after a Mayday signal
from the rig.
TRICKY
At 6.45 am. he took off from
a Scarborough helicopter pad.
He flew out to the rig and landed
in howling winds.
He picked up 19 men and
transferred them to the Con-
stellation after a tricky landing.
Then he flew back to Ocean
Prince to pick up 18 men, whom
he took back to Constellation.
Back he went to Ocean Prince
to pick up the remaining 8 men
and take them ashore.
He deliberately did not refuel
until the final stage of the
rescue because he was overload-
ing the helicopter and balancing
the extra weight by running low
on fuel.
Captain Balls, of Ashby-cum-
Fenby, near Grimsby, said later:

PROPERTY OF 
 DAILY HERALD 
 RCD. 3 - JUL 1951 
 PLEASE RETURN 
 TO

SECRETS OF THE CHINESE 
 IN THE KILNS OF CHEYNE ROW   DG/ PM 
 Visitors to the Loan Exhibition of 
 Chelsea China at the Royal Hospital, 
 Chelsea this month and next, will have 
 an opportunity to see some of the best work 
 of MR CHARLES VYSE the famous Chelsea potter. 
 The work on show is proof enough that the 
 Vyse kilns in Cheyne Row, are every bit as 
 productive as were those in Lawrence street 
 and Justice Walk in the heyday of the famous 
 Chelsea China factory over 200 years ago. 
 With his colleague Barbara Waller, Mr Vyse has 
 rediscovered the secret of the pottery of the 
 fabulous Chinese Sung Dynasty, a secret lost 
 to the Chinese long ago, and known nowhere 
 in Europe save in Cheyne Row. 
 PHOTO SHOWS:- BARBARA WALLER examines 
 the "May Queen" to see that her enamel 
 painting has fired up correctly 
 FOX PHOTOS  July 2 1951 44/433

activity: Members of the Mellor family re-thatching Maerdy Farm house and celebrating a 21st birthday.

te.text:
Stephens, Cardiff.  D.H.  2.11.56.
THATCHER 'ON THE TILES'
Thatching has been the work of the Mellor family
from Burton on Trent for generations. When their
father died nearly twenty years ago Harry Mellor
was faced with the task of carrying on the craft and
training his three younger brothers. Now the four
brothers travel all over the country, doing their
skilled work. This week, while three of them work
re-thatching Maerdy Farm house at Rumney, near
Cardiff, the youngest brother, Fred celebrated his
21st birthday. After he had carried the last load
of reeds up to his brothers Fred carried up his
celebration ale. He is the youngest craftsman in
the business, they think.
O.P.S. Fred Mellor takes a bundle of reeds to 25
year old William.

O.P.S. The brothers drink at toast. Top Harry (34)
William(25,) and Fred(21.)

activity: A children's nurse resting under a chestnut tree in Kensington Gardens during a sunny weekend.

te.text:
Alarm

FINALLY, Miss and Mr. Everyman.
Miss Everyman was Edna Pickthall,
25-year-old children's nurse, of Bays-
water. She spoke of her day as she
basked under a
chestnut tree in
Kensington Gar-
dens. Carol, three
years old, rolled
on the grass.
" This is likely
to be the one quiet
moment until this
evening, I'm
afraid.
" You see, when
I woke this morn-
ing we found that Carol's sister had
measles, and that meant a hurried break-
fast—tea and toast and cereals—and a
visit from the doctor, and all the business
of the sickroom, and the job of keeping
Carol away from infection.
" Still, the evening's ahead, and isn't
spring good? "

TOMLIN
6.3.38
SUNSHINE WEEK END SCENES.
Miss Edna Pickthall a nursemaid,
of 12 Bark Place, Bayswater.

PAUL - became demonstrably possessive. [illegible] was not 
 [illegible]ough for him to see this wonder of wonders, he 
 [illegible]anted it for himself, for keeps. But that just 
 [illegible]an't be done. Other little patients at Great 
 [illegible]rmond Street will enjoy this 'escape to happiness' 
 [illegible]n the future, too, for the Hospital's work is 
 [illegible]nceasing.

JOHN - "who just won't sit down for anyone or anything"

 his cot, transfixed, immobile and open-mouthed with 
 sheer wonderment. His shoe-button eyes grew larger and 
 larger under the influence of this new experience.

activity: the Ferguson 35 de-luxe (Diesel Model) tractor

te.text:
ART LIBRARY
PLEASE RETURN
TO
DAILY HERALD
20 OCT 1956

E M B A R G O
NOT TO BE PUBLISHED BEFORE 4.00 p.m. ON MONDAY,
October 1st, 1956

NEW FERGUSON TRACTOR - the FERGUSON 35 de-luxe (Diesel Model)

The Ferguson 35 de-luxe incorporates numerous entirely new features
resulting from 13 years of intense research. The famous Ferguson hydraulic
system has been revolutionised. In addition to raising and lowering an
implement and automatically keeping a plough or cultivator at a selected
depth on uneven ground, the new hydraulic system gives the tractor driver
perfect control of front, mid or rear-mounted implements.

A new dual clutch gives a "live", engine-driven power-take-off for
power driven implements such as mowers or balers. A six speed gear box pro-
vides a wide selection of gears for every job on the farm enabling full use
to be made of the 37 brake h.p.. An alternative, ground speed p.t.o. in
hay making or fertilising, irrespective of the gear selected.

Among the many other important new features are included more
precise and easier steering, two steering brake pedals on the right hand
side of the transmission housing, a new safety starter, safety fuel tank,
instrument panel with a combined tachometer, speedometer and hour meter,
foamed cushion seat and padded back rest. Also new is the styling in two-tone
Ferguson grey and metallic bronze.

te.text:
16965I(CHI). NEW SHERVIK TRACTOR DEMONSTRATES EQUIPMENT
FOR USE IN EAST AFRICAN GROUNDNUTS SCHEME.

BAGSHOT(Surrey)ENG: A demonstration of the new Shervik
tractor, which has been specially designed for work on
the British Government's East African groundnut scheme,
was held near here. The new tractor, built by
Vickers-Armstrongs Ltd, combines certain of the components
of the Sherman Mark V tank, including one of the two-stroke
Diesel engines.
All the tractors are fitted with a universal "U" frame
to which a variety of implements can be fitted. Stumper
blades are used for digging out tree stumps with their
roots, and trees can be quickly uprooted by the use of
the treedozer. After the root-cutter has been at work
collection of the roots is accomplished with a rootrake,
16 feet in width.
"PHOTO SHOWS: - A Shervik tractor easily pushing down a
tree with the use of the treedozer, during the demonstration.

"Homes Convoy" lorries in as
many minutes—carrying sec-
tions of aluminium bungalows
to all parts of the South.
9½ in a minute
It is just over two years since
Airoh bungalow No. 1 left this
factory, which produced Beau-
fighters during the war. Today
these cream and green prefabs are
leaving Oldmixon at the rate of 30
a day from the conveyor belt
where No. 6886 was born.
"Life" for No. 6886 started on
Thursday at 8 a.m. when its floors,
in four sections,
were con-
structed in Old
Nixon's No. 7
workshop. Later
in the day the
floors were
moved by over-
head crane to
the conveyor
belt for assem-
bly of kitchen
and bathroom units.
Moved by tractor to No. 8 work-
shop, No. 6886 acquired its walls,
windows, doors, and roof as its
four parts moved 9½ inches a
minute down the assembly lines.
On Friday, at 7.45 a.m., No. 6886
was about to enter the factory's
huge paint-spraying tunnel, where
the paint is treated with hot and
cold air.
At 10.15 it was driven out of the
factory
And at 3 p.m. it left the factory
gates—less than 20 hours after its
first part was assembled.
I talked to the four drivers
taking No. 6886 to Ockenden—an
11½ hours run. Ex-RAF "Erk"
Roy Shingfield said: "When
I drive along with a part of one
of these houses I think: 'Some
lucky one has got a home to live
in.'"
Roy is hoping to get married
next year, if he can get a house.

"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED

te.text:
AIMED AT THE EXPORT TARGET: 
BOWS OF STEEL ARROWS OF ALUMINIUM    DG/HT

     If Robin Hood and his Merry Men  could return
to their legendary haunts under the Greenwood Tree,
they would be surprised to find that  their stout
yew bows  had been superseded by superior weapons
of the finest steel.  Arrows too, are no longer the
grey goose feathered shafts   which routed the French
at Agincourt.    The bowman of 1950 uses aluminium.
     With the export market  as their target, a well
known steel tubing firm in Birmingham (Messrs. Accles
and Pollock) are now making  the new  bows and arrows
in steel and aluminium.  The steel  long bows are
said by expert archers, to give   far better performance
and greater accuracy than wooden weapons. Orders for
them  have  been coming in from all parts of the world.
     Making the bows, involves 200 processes, almost
everyone byhand. Fourteen heat treatments   are needed
and the  thickness of the tapered steel tube from which
the bow is drawn has to be controlled within one-thousandth
of an inch.

PHOTO SHOWS:- "Bow-belle". This young lady is putting
the crest on the aluminium arrows at the factory, before
they are exported.

FOX PHOTOS   Jan 22nd 1950 413237

by the coal shortage. Stocks of fuel are said to be so low that it
will be impossible to start work again unless the present allocation
is revised and delivery increased, and the works may be closed for
several weeks.
With coal distribution crippled by blizaards, hundreds of industrial
plants throughout Britain have had to close down temporarily, and many
thousands of workers have been thrown out of work.
PHOTO SHOWS:- The silent and deserted finishing shop with uncompleted
vehicles on the assembly lines at the Austin Motor Company's works at
Longbridge, Birmingham.

activity: a member of the Women's Land Army cutting a forked twig from a hazel tree to use for water divining

te.text:
ESTEN                                  ILLUS.                  10.6.42
LAND GIRL DISCOVERED AS WATER DIVINER.
It has taken the Women's Land Army to find out
that Miss Littler, a volunteer in the employment
of the Flintshire War Agricultural Executive
Committee possesses the gift of water divining.
Miss Littler joined the Women's Land Army March 1941
and is one of 9 girls employed on gang work.
Recently they were working on a piece of land which
was constantly being flooded by a hidden spring.
Mr.J.T.Richards, the Executive Officer of the
Flintshire War Agricultural Executive Committee, had
made extensive efforts to have the spring located.
Finally, he asked the 9 members of the Women's Land
Army, who were clearing the land, to try with a
hazel stick to see if they could divine this spring.
Miss Littler was found to be the only one who
possesses this unusual gift.
Since Flintshire farmers have heard of this there
have been many requests for her services, to help
in reclaiming flooded land and so save hundreds
of pounds in drainage. Also farmers wish to use
her to help to discover water for sinking wells.
O.P.S.1.  The first step to becoming a Diviner
is to cut a forked twig from a hazel tree.
Miss Littler who is 19 years of age is seen on
right.

Last night outside the House of Commons as police close St. Stephen's entrance against the huge crowd trying to get to the Lobbies.
HERALD REPORTER
THE girl from behind the Post Office counter, the little lady who types those polite demands "Dear Sir, unless ..." and 3,000 other women from Government offices packed Central Hall, Westminster last night. 
With one voice they declared: "We want equal pay." A smattering of men came along to back them.
Mr. Hugh Gaitskell, Chancellor of the Exchequer, has already said the Government accepts the principal, but that nothing can be done about it at this critical period, as it would have a serious inflationary affect.

te.text:
ESTATE FOR ALL INCOMES.
First turf on the site of a London County Council community estate, to cater for higher as well as lower income groups, was cut by Mr.I.J. Hayward, a leader of the L.C.C.
The 72 "middle income" houses included in the St Paul's Cray estate will be built in pairs, each with a garden back and front, a drive and garage.
Downstairs there will be a hall, cloakroom, large sittingroom and lounge separated by sliding doors, dining room and modern kitchen.
Upstairs will be four large bedrooms and bathroom.
The houses will be let at an economic rent of between £130 and £150 a year, exclusive of rates.
The 570 acre estate will have 3,883 dwellings altogether and include three-storey blocks of flats, five modern schools, churches, shops, a cinema, public-house, parks and a large playground. It will cost £5,500,000.

activity: The Queen signing the Sentence of Consecration at the new Cathedral Church of St. Michael.

te.text:
THE Consecration
of the new
Cathedral Church
of St. Michael here
today was a cere-
money of simple,
yet luxurious
beauty.
The simplicity was in
the small, central acts
of consecration; the
luxury was in the
splendour of the set-
ting, the richness of
the ritual.
AWE
There were first the
processions, 11 of them in
all, containing a Queen, a
Princess, nine arch-
bishops, a stiffening of
knights, innumerable am-
bassadors.
Last but one came the
Queen's procession, pre-
ceded by her Gentlemen-
at-Arms, those clinking,
grey old gentlemen who
supply these occasions
with a sort of instant awe.
YELLOW
The Queen, in yellow,
was received at the gate
of the old cathedral by
the Bishop of Coventry,
Dr. Cuthbert Bardsley,
and escorted to the west
door of the new.
In her procession
walked Sir Basil Spence,
the Cathedral architect.
Fanfares, drums, and
then, as they died down,
the business of consecra-
tion. A technical cere-
mony, which begins,
superbly, with the Bishop
shouting "Open the
door."
The small unconcealing
glass doors swing open
and the Bishop, hitherto
seen but unheard, is es-
corted in.

The Queen signs the Sentence of Consecration. Her name as first wit-
ness is followed by that of the Archbishop of Canterbury, Dr. Ramsey.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
26 MAY 1962
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

activity: The upstream face of Clunie dam, now nearly completed.

te.text:
HIGHLAND POWER SCHEME NEARLY READY
Cpr. 25.10.49.
The North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board's Tummel-Garry
scheme, is expected to go into operation at the end of this
year when parts of the Clunie dam are completed. The 386 foot
long and 65 foot high Clunie dam at the Eastern end of Loch
Tummel will raise the level of the Loch by 17 feet and
more than double its length. The water will flow through a
23 foot diameter tunnel for two miles to the Clunie Power
Station, where three turbo-alternators with a total capacity
of 57,000kws, will be in operation. To equalise the fluctuating
discharge from Clunie Power Station will be the primary
function of the 480 foot long 74 foot high dam at Pitlochry.
Here, the power station is incorporated in the dam, and two turbo-
alternators will have a generating capacity of 15,000 kws.
Both dams have a fish ladder to enable salmon to reach the
upper reaches of the River Tummel. The whole scheme will have
an annual output of about 300 million units, and will have
another dam on the upper reaches of the River Errochty which
will have a high water level nearly 1,100 feet above sea-
level. The picture shows:-

No.1. The upstream face of Clunie dam, now nearly completed.
The concrete structure has been painted black to forestall any
action of the peaty water, and to seal any minute cracks in the
face of the wall. Note the tiny figure of a workman half-way
up the face [illegible] on the right hand side.

COPYRIGHT PHOTO ISSUED BY
CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
119, FLEET STREET, LONDON, E.C.4
CENTRAL 2266/7.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF
'DAILY HERALD' AND MUST BE
RETURNED TO THE ART LIBRARY BY
JAN 20 1950
Indus Fuel & Power - Electr - Water Power.

te.text:
NEW STEEL FROM THE SCRAP HEAP.    AW/AT

There is now a tremendous demand for scrap metal, which is
fetching a good price. These pictures were taken at a
Letchworth foundry where scrap steel is analysed on arrival
and the best quality cut into short lengths with oxy-acetelene
flames. It is then fed into cupolas where it becomes molten
iron. This iron is then transformed into high quality steel
by a battery of "converters" and turned into anything from
an engine wheel to a ship's davit.

Photo shows:- Cutting up old locomotive wheels ready for
melting in the cupolas.

te.text:
LN 269016      TEA        LONDON BUREAU
BUILD THEIR OWN HOMES IN SPARE TIME.

LONDON: Clerks, builders, printing workers and
lorry drivers are among the 25 members of the
Camberwell Enterprise Housing Club, who are
building their own homes on a site at Crystal
Palace (South London). The idea was born two
years ago, now every night, and at weekends
and holidays, the men work on the houses.
Neighbours lend a hand and much of the work
is done at night with the aid of floodlights.
Special features of the homes will be a modified
form of central heating; a garage to each house;
and a new "Accotile" plastic tile flooring
throughout. Skilled, unpaid foreman is Bill
Clark, who with Len King, a building representative
during the day, works in the "site" hut with the
plans. Bill will be the first to move into one
of the new homes - in May. The project is expected
to be completed in two years time.
PHOTO SHOWS: LEN KING - a building representative
in the daytime - tests the door jambs of one of
the houses. REG BRUCE, a paint worker, and HARRY OTT
(right), a printer, lay bricks.

Planet News Feature Service, 1954 PN-d

DAILY HERALD

activity: Residents in the open-plan and fenced gardens of a housing development.

te.text:
HOW would you like to move into a new luxury £4,600 home without a lawn of your own, a front gate or a fence to gossip over?
Open-plan houses like this are already a common feature of suburban life in America, Canada and Australia; on a smaller scale, they are also found on council estates in Britain.
But now, because of the high cost of land on private developments, "togetherness" living is spreading among the young families who are buying a brand new home of their own.
Castles
If you live on one of these estates, you share the expenses of a gardener to mow the communal lawn, the upkeep of service roads, shared drive-ins and planned gardens.
Traditionally, we British like our "castles." We fence ourselves in and keep the neighbours out with a privet hedge and a stout front gate.
But the old attitude is already changing in the face of the high cost of seclusion on the new building developments. Damer Gardens in Henley-on-Thames, Oxfordshire, is typical of these new developments.
Back gardens are divided by post and rail fences, though some residents are already reinforcing these with barriers of wattle.

DAILY HERALD

activity: Exploratory oil drilling in Lancashire, showing mud circulation from deep bore holes.

te.text:
DcH White 13/7/49
Oil search at Formby
8/ Sam Bromley watches mud circulating
from 216 ft below ground being brought
up to surface

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNREPAIRED.

SEARCH FOR OIL IN LANCASHIRE.
Somewhere beneath the sand-dunes of the Lancashire
coast, seven miles from Southport, lies a huge
untapped supply of oil.
Sixteen engineers who have just sunk a bore hole hope
to find it before their instruments register 7,500 ft.
They cannot go any deeper than that with their present
equipment and if they have not found it at that depth
they will try somewhere else.
An official at the D'Arcy Exploration Co, who is doing
the work, said "for ten years we have been getting 400
tons of oil a year from eight 'surface wells' at
Formby, but those wells are only 100 ft deep and we are
confident that a large oilfield, much deeper is
supplying them".
They tried three times before at Scarisbrick and
Bickerstaffe, but although they went down to 7,600 ft
they could not find the source.
Pointing to a thick, pinky fluid oozing out of a large
pipe alongside the towering derrick on the new site,
John Gibson the drilling superintendant explained
"that is the circulating mud which we pour down the
centre of the drill pipe, It seeps through the drilling
bit and brings up the small pieces of rock formation".
After the formation has been sieved out, the mud goes
back down the drill pipe.

te.text:
FIRST STAGE OF BLACKWALL TUNNEL DUPLICATION SCHEME.
21.4.58
London E.1.
Road work in connection with the London County Council's
scheme for the improvement of the Northern approach
to the Blackwall Tunnel-the first stage of the project
for the duplication of the Tunnel-began today. Mr
A.A. Nugent, Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Transport, started the work on the site, bounded by
East India Dock Road, Brusnwick Road, Drew Street and
St Leonards Road, today. The total cost of the improvements
is estimated at £1,600,000- including road works,
aquisition of property and rehousing of displaced families.
It is expected that the work will be completed by the end
of 1960.

I.N.P. PHOTO SHOWS: Mr A.A. Nugent, Parliamentary Secretary
to the Ministry of Transport, is instructed in
driving a Bulldozer by Mr Hughie Gallagher,
when he started the work on the site today.
Picture by Monte Fresco Jnr.
TDH/122883 INTERNATIONAL NEWS PHOTOS.

PROPERTY OF

 DG/RS

activity: Labourers hand-sowing barley seed at Tillingdown Farm during the spring battle for harvest.

te.text:
BROADCASTING THE SPRING SEED........
BATTLE FOR THE HARVEST BEGINS IN BRITAIN.

With the first few sunny days of Spring sunshine, farmers
all over Britain are ploughing and sowing with all speed to gain
the valuable time lost through floods and tempest throughout the
land..   More than six weeks have been lost through severe
Winter weather, and the farmers and their labourers toil from
dawn till dusk in the great battle for the harvest - sorely needed -
which is to follow their present efforts.
Down on Sir Peter Greenwell's estate at Caterham, Surrey, the
ground, still heavy with moisture, would not be ready for sowing
by mechanical means for several days to come - but time is precious
and the sowing is being done by hand to gain valuable hours........
PHOTO SHOWS:- Scattering the seed.   Labourers broadcasting barley
seed by hand at Tillingdown Farm, Caterham, Surrey.
Caterham village can be seen in background.
DAW.                 13th April, 1947.          PN-s.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

PLANET NEWS LTD

te.text: Housing - Flats and new Estates. (See also - London - Southwark)

NOT TO BE PUBLISHED BEFORE SATURDAY, DEC. 17th.
16.12.60.
PREVIEW OF BRANDON ESTATE, SOUTHWARK.
TO BE OPENED TOMORROW.

Brandon Estate, Southwark, a major L.C.C.
project combining the rehabilitation of nearly 200
old houses with the provision of over 1,000 new
dwellings ranging from old persons' bungalows to
18-storey point blocks, will be opened tomorrow (Dec.
17) by the Chairman of the L.C.C. (Mrs. F.E. Cayford).
The estate is one of the largest of the L.C.C.'s
redevelopment schemes for inner London, and is the
first example of the L.C.C.'s policy of infusing new
life into decaying areas of London's "middle belt"
by combining the complete redevelopment of the property
in worst condition with thorough modernisation of
property still in sound structural order. There is
accommodation for 5,000 people, and the estimated total
cost of the work is £3,596,450.

KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:- Interior view showing
the [struck through] living room in the flat occupied
by Mr. and Mrs. Lewington - at today's preview
of the estate.

H/Keystone EM/725097

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
17 DEC 1960
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

Teifi at Cenarth was closed at the start
of the war, most people thought that its
days were ended.

the mill has been overhauled and is once
more producing whole-meal flour for making
into bread that is in great demand in
the local bakehouses.

before the war, and who works there
occasionally now, watches the wholemeal
flour pouring once again from the stones.

activity: Female engineering apprentice Barbara Hampson working among male apprentices at a Huddersfield company.

te.text:
ENGINEERING JILL IMPROVES THEIR SKILL
October 30th 1968 PAP 136427-1 (PNR/P-D)

============================================

ENGINEERING JILL IMPROVES THEIR SKILL

     The best way , it would seem, to spur
on engineering apprentices to greater
effort, is to put a girl among the boys.
You can't stop them stealing admiring
glances at BARBARA HAMPSON, 18, -  she is
herself an apprentice at a Huddersfield
engineering company - but the 16 boy
apprentices work harder than ever. They
are determined not to be outdone in their
engineering skills by a member of the
opposite sex.
     The senior instructor at the school,
Mr. Brian Glendinning, declares that
Huddersfield's only girl engineering
apprentice is really keeping the boys
on their toes and, with a girl around
there is no bad language , even when a
boy drops a spanner on his toe.
     Barbara joined the firm from school,
after obtaining six G.C.E. "O" Levels,
including one for metalwork and another
for technical drawing. She wants to
become a draughtsman one day and said "I was
a bit worried at first among so many boys.
They tease me unmercifully but I'm getting
used to it".
October 30th 1968 PAP 136427-1 (PNR/P-D)

PRESS ASSOCIATION PHOTOS.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN EVENING
PAPERS OF  WEDNESDAY OCTOBER 30th 1968

SUN
PROPERTY

activity: unloading raw rubber bales from the ship 'Benlawers' onto a barge at Tilbury Docks

te.text:
FIRST POST-WAR CARGOES OF RAW RUBBER ARRIVE IN ENGLAND.

The first raw rubber cargoes to reach this country from Malaya for
nearly four years are being discharged in London docks. At Tilbury
Dock a cargo of about 580 tons of rubber has been unloaded from
the "Benlawers" - a transhipment from Singapore, picked up at
Calcutta. It is the second shipment to be made by the Rubber Control
buying unit.  The first, a small shipment of 150 tons which was
brought by the "Almanzora" to Southampton, was held up by the
dockers' strike and finally reached London by rail. A third
consignment of 300 tons from Singapore was brought into Liverpool
by the "Clan Chisholm". A fourth - and much larger - rubber cargo
of 8,300 tons left Singapore on board the "Empire" on October 28th.
PHOTO SHOWS:- A cargo of raw rubber from Malaya being unloaded
from the "Benlawers" onto a barge at Tilbury Docks, Essex: the
bales of rubber, which weigh about 280 lbs. apiece, are swung
overboard in nets, and manoeuvred into place on the barge.
DAV 21 November 1945 PN

COPYRIGHT
PLANET NEWS LTD.
3 JOHNSON'S COURT,
FLEET STREET, E.C.4.
PHONE: CENTRAL 3671-3

te.text:
BERKSHIRE.

THE THATCHERS ARE BUSY.

In the quiet villages of Berkshire and Wiltshire the
thatchers are busy carrying out spring repairs on
farms and cots and age-old barns. There are plenty of
thatched roofs in this part of England and there is no
lack of work for the craftsmen in villages where sometimes
nearly every other roof is a thatch.

Photo shows- Mr. Adams and his son at work on a thatched
roof at Shrivenham which shelters half a dozen homes. It
has more than 6,200 square feet of thatch and seven tons
of straw were used on it. Mr. Adams is a busy man these days.
Fox April 2nd. 36.

SPRING THATCHING
Thatchers at work on a picturesque row
of cottages at Shrivenham, Berks. The
last few years have seen a welcome
revival in this rural industry, which at-
one time seemed in danger of dying out.

SWORDS FOR THE CORONATION.         AW/HT

The day of the sword as a weapon of war is over, but
swords are still used in the services for parades and
ceremonial occasions.  Swords for officers and high
personages and members of Diplomatic Corps who will
be taking part in the forthcoming Coronation ceremonies
are now being prepared by the Wilkinson Sword Company
of Chiswick, who have been making swords since 1772.
Most swords are engraved with a Service badge with the
King's initials forming part of the design on the King's
cipher.

Photo shows:-   Tom Beasley, a steel craftsman, wearing
the hat of the sword forger, seen forging a sword at
Chiswick.
Fox Jany 15th. 37.

NURSERY LANE SITE - HALLAMSHIRE HOUSES

Councillor Albert King, leader of the Leeds City Council, opened the first 40
factory built houses to be built on the Nursery Lane site at Moortown; more than
230 industrialised dwellings of various types are planned in the city during 1963-
64 and more than 500 in 1964-65.

These houses represent a transition between traditional construction and a fully
prefabricated system as being investigated by the Yorkshire Development Group.
(Founder members are Leeds, Sheffield and Hull, new members - Nottingham and
Scunthorpe. The group hope to speed-up and reduce the costs of municipal house
building by using industrialised methods of construction). Forty houses are
being erected in terraces on this site.

The houses are of the five-person three-bedroomed type and above the 'Parker
Morris' minimum standards as described in the Ministry of Housing and Local Govern-
ment's publication 'Homes for Today and Tomorrow'.
