activity: a cart horse named Bunny escaping and being captured during a film shoot for a television transmission of Tristan und Isolade at Alexandra Palace

te.text:
ROPER.
14.1.38.
BUNNY THE CART HORSE ESCAPES.
When an outdoor film sequence was made
this morning at Alexandra Palace, Bunny
the cart horse threw his rider, who was
King Marke, and escaped. The King's knights
and bodyguard chased Bunny all over the Palace
grounds, and eventually captured him, but
film work was held up for an hour. The film
will be merged into hunting scenes to be
interpolated in the television transmission
of 'Tristan und [illegible] Isolade' on January 24.
P.S.
Bunny the cart horse captured, would not be
led back to the film set so George had to
ride him back.

title: A photographic print of Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip, Visit to Newport, October, 1962

date_info.rationale: Stamps likely indicate processing or publication date.

activity: The Queen opening the Richard Thomas and Baldwin's steelworks at Llanwern.

te.text:
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
27 OCT 1962
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

BY BASIL MORGAN
THE Queen pressed a small brass button yesterday—and set moving the giant rollers of Britain's most modern steelworks.
Then she watched the first 10-ton ingot start a spectacular half-mile journey to end up as a steel strip 100 yards long.
She was opening Richard Thomas and Baldwin's new £150million steelworks at Llanwern, near Newport, Monmouthshire.
It was a ceremony that nearly did not take place.
On Thursday night, an electrical fault put the whole chain of hot steel rollers out of action.
PUT RIGHT
An emergency squad of repair men worked through the night and on into the morning. They put the fault right only hours before the Queen arrived.
Later the Queen, who was accompanied by Prince Philip, saw the steelworks' computor room, where all processes are automatically tracked.
She took over one set of controls and altered the thickness of sheet steel being made for Jaguar cars.
From Hot Mills to High Jinks — that's the name of a five-year-old pony the Queen has bought for Princess Anne. An announcement last night said that the pony has already been delivered to the Royal Stables.

title: A photographic print of Industry, Sword Making

date_info.rationale: Stamp indicates receipt by press library.

activity: Inspection of Royal Air Force Guard of Honour swords.

te.text:
THE RETURN OF THE SWORD

Coronation Brings It Back to Popularity

The sword, ancient weapon of defence, has now
become a token of ceremony. It will be much in
evidence during the Coronation festivities.
Many sword cutlers have gone out of business
in this age of the atom, but one firm, The
Wilkinson Sword Company, of Acton, London, have
kept up the ancient industry. At present they
have orders for 2,000 swords. They are busy making
officers' ceremonial swords or refurbishing old ones
that will be used in the Coronation.
Some of the orders received have come from Overseas.
The firm has the market largely to itself
- even American manufacturers appear to have
gone out of business.
Ceremonial swords have not been a standard item
of officers' equipment in the Army since before the
war. Many orders have been placed by the Ministry
of Supply and service-owned swords are issued to
officers as required from a pool formed by
regiments. Nevertheless, many officers still possess
pre-war swords and hundreds of these have been
sent for renovation, which mostly involves
replating. The average cost of this work is about
£5.
Many existing swords, including those belonging
to the Yeomen of the Guard, are being sent to the
firm to be brought up to date and embossed
with the Queen's cipher.

I.N.P. PHOTO SHOWS:- Long line of Royal Air Force
Guard of Honour swords are laid out for
final inspection by Mrs Anne Bourchier, of
Chiswick, (left) and Mrs. Doris Spenceley of
Shepherds Bush.
BYL/FS 4511-2. INTERNATIONAL NEWS PHOTOS.

te.text:
YOUNG DUTCH CRAFTSMAN AT
SUSSEX POTTERIES.   MJH/FM.

At the Rye Potteries (Rye, Sussex) many youngsters
are employed, in an effort to foster and encourage
artistic skill in the younger generation. These young
craftsmen show much natural skill only surpassed by
their enthusiasm. Among these youngsters at the Potteries
is Herman Zaalberg, an 18-years-old Dutch boy from
Leiderdorp, who is paying a 12-months visit to this
country to learn our methods and designs in the Pottery
craft. Herman hopes to take over the family pottery,
now being run by his father in Holland, which was
started by his grandfather.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:  The young Dutch potter 18-years-old
Herman Zaalberg from Leiderdorp, seen at work in the
Potteries at Rye Sussex.

te.text:
PUSS POTTER.
MJH/MJH.
As she works in her pottery at Kensington (W. London),
Miss Maisie Seneshall is surrounded by cats of all sizes,
all colours, all breeds and in a variety of poses, but there
is never a purr or a mew.  For these cats are now real, they
are the result of Miss Seneshall's skill as a potter, for
she specialises in pottery cats, finding a ready market for
this work both in this country and overseas.  Miss
Seneshall's models are "true to life" for she sketches cats
in various poses at Cat Shows, etc, to give authenticity to her
work.
PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:  MISS MAISIE SENESHALL seen putting two
of her cat models - a Siamese and a tabby - into the kiln
for firing at her Kensington (W. London) pottery.

activity: View of the ship Tiger being dismantled in a ship breaking yard.

te.text:
WH
THE GRAVEYARD OF THE SEA GIANTS.
A remarkable sight meets the eye at the ship breaking yard
of Thomas Ward, Ltd, at Inverkeithing. Ships no longer look
like ships, rather do they resemble masses of old iron. It is
difficult to believe that ships like the Cedric and the Tiger
once the pride of their services could be reduced to their
present state in the short space of six weeks. But such is the
destructiveness of man, and shortly they will both be
reduced to their last bolt.
Photo shows- A general view of the Tiger in the hands of the
shipbreaker- a view that few Naval men would recognise as being
the famous Tiger.
FOX May/9th.32.

activity: reconstruction of a shooting in a church hall

te.text:
FULL STORY OF HOW A GUNMAN YESTERDAY FIRED
AT A VICAR, A VERGER AND A POSTMAN IN A LONDON
CHURCH HALL, SHOT THE VICAR IN THE CHEEK AND
THEN KILLED HIMSELF WAS TOLD TO THE " DAILY
HERALD " LAST NIGHT BY THE VERGER.
The dead man was identified late at night as Mr. Alfred
Stanley Kirby, a 26-year-old printer, of Derwent-avenue,
Edmonton, N.
Scene of this " murder attempt without a motive, " as a
police official described it, was the hall of St. John's Church,
Vartry-road, Stamford Hill, N.

THESE TWO " Daily Herald " pictures reconstruct the shooting in the church
hall. First the assailant fired through the stage curtains at Mr. Walter
Longhurst, the verger, as shown above; then he appeared through the door
(left) at the side of the stage to shoot at the vicar, before returning to the
stage, climbing a ladder and killing himself.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RCD. 26 JUL 1950
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

SHORTAGE OF MANPOWER
DOESN'T STOP THIS EXPORT DRIVE DG/W2

While MISS GERTRUDE GILHAM works at the
potters wheel, making vases for export,
her sister provides the "manpower" on a wheel
which drives the turntable. This system of
driving the potters wheel is an ancient one
and the little factory in Poole, Dorset, is possibly
unique in its use. Miss Gilham has been
in the craft for over 25 yrs.

FOX PHOTOS July 25th 1950

COPYRIGHT
FOX
PHOTOS
LTD.
6, TUDOR ST.,
LONDON, E.C.

activity: men at work on a huge merchant vessel nearing completion in a shipyard during World War II

te.text:
SHIPYARD WORKERS BEAT THE U-BOATS.         WS/X

While the Navy and the Air Force are beating Hitler's
U-boats by direct action, the men of the shipyards of
this country are defeating them in another way - by
building merchant ships which replace the ones that
have been sunk. Every few days we launch a merchant
ship from one of our shipyards, and it is reassuring
to know that we can build ships faster than the enemy
can sink them.

Photo shows - A striking picture showing men at work
on the huge vessel nearing completion in the shipyard.
PASSED BY CENSOR.
FOX. FEB. 26th. 40. (NP 1400)

FOX PHOTOS LTD.
6, TUDOR ST.
LONDON, E.C.4.

activity: inspection of a dismantled Morris Mini-Minor engine after a 100,000-mile oil trial

te.text:
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
--8 MAR 1962
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

ENGINE STRIPPED AFTER 100,000 MILES TEST
March 8th 1962 PAR XX94991-2 (Sa-G)

The engine of a Morris Mini-Minor
dismantled and laid out for inspection
at the BP Research Establishment at
Sunbury-on-Thames, Middlesex, to-day
(Thursday) at the end of a 100,000 miles
'static' motor oil proving trial for BP 'Visco-
static' motor oil.
MR. J. CLYDESALE, Foreman Mechanic,
is inspecting one of the parts. He was
responsible for all routine service
checks during the trial.
Six production cars, selected at random
from showrooms by the RAC, took part
in the test. They were a Ford Anglia,
Hillman Minx, 3.8 Jaguar, Morris Mini-
Minor, Triumph Herald 1200 and a
Vauxhall Velox. All successfully
completed the 100,000 miles, which
began on May 1st last year after all
the engines had been sealed.
Most of the driving was done on the
M 1 Motorway but the cars were also
taken on to town and country roads, and
hill climbs also featured in the trial.
The engines were stripped down under
RAC supervision at Sunbury-on-Thames.
March 8th 1962. PAR XX 94991-2 (Sa-G)

No reproduction fee:

Issued with the compliments of the
BRITISH PETROLEUM COMPANY
INDUS - MOTOR CAR - TESTING - RESEARCH - ETC

activity: Idle car assembly lines at the Rover Works due to coal shortages.

te.text:
SHORTAGE OF COAL BRINGS BRITAIN'S BIG INDUSTRY
TO STANDSTILL
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
4-2-47

The big Midlands car factory, the Rover Works, Birmingham
has been paralysed owing to the coal shortage. Cars for
export and home market were being made here. Day by day they
moved off the production line, till coal stocks dwindled
to nothing, as consumption, even with every economy, out-
distanced supply. Like many other factories, these works
are paralysed by the coal shortage, and the plant stood
silent for three days.
I.N.P. PHOTO SHOWS: No coal - so the rotors stand idle
and no car has moved forward on
the assembly lines.

SPECIAL.
117/J. 6061
INTERNATIONAL NEWS PHOTOS

date_info.rationale: This date is typed at the end of the news caption, indicating when the copy was prepared for dispatch.

activity: Men working on the spacious interior of the 'Brabazon's' main passenger cabin.

te.text:
126-TON 'BRABAZON' NEARS COMPLETION, WILL FLY THIS SUMMER.

Under the hands of 700 workers, the world's biggest landplane
is nearing completion at the plant of the Bristol Aeroplane
Company at Filton, Bristol.
Designed to be the aerial counterpart of the 'Queen Elizabeth' -
world's greatest ocean liner - the plane is the 'Brabazon I',
the gigantic sections of which are almost ready for final assembly.
It is expected that the 126-ton monster will take the air
for the first time in May or June and that three other
Brabazons on order will be flying on the London-New York service
of British Overseas Airways by 1950.
The Brabazon is a high-altitude, long-range low-wing cantilever
monoplane which will accommodate 70 to 100 sleeping passengers
or 120 sitting passengers in the utmost comfort.  The
143-feet cabin will be pressurised to maintain an equivalent
cabin altitude of 8,000 feet while flying at 25,000 feet.
Crew will number 13, including five stewards.
Wingspan of the aircraft is 230 feet - almost twice that
of Britain's largest bomber, the Avro Lincoln - and the height
over the rudder is 50 feet.
Eight Bristol 'Centaurus' 18-cylinder, sleeve-valve,
air-cooled radial engines, each rated at 2,500 brake horsepower
for take-off, will give a maximum level speed of more than 300
miles an hour at 25,000 feet, and economical cruising speed
of 250 miles an hour at the same altitude, and a still-air range
of 5,000 miles.  Initial service ceiling will be 25,000 feet,
increasing as fuel is consumed.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Men working on the spacious interior of the
'Brabazon's' main passenger cabin.
AND March 31st 1947 PN.r.

MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

activity: combined harvester and wagon emptying grain in Alberta

te.text:
WONDERFUL LABOUR SAVING DEVICE USED IN
CANADIAN HARVESTING.

EIGHT THOUSAND BUSHELS PER DAY CUT AND THRASHED
BY ONE MACHINE WITHOUT BINDING AND STOOKING.

What is believed to have been the greatest use made of
mechanical power in farming ever witnessed in Western
Canada was used in the recent harvesting at Aldersyde
Alberta. A combined reaping and threshing machine was
used which dispenses with the idea of cutting in the
first place and the usual stooking by hand labour for
sun drying. This machine is used when the wheat
is dry and is out, thrown in the thresher and the wheat
transferred into a huge tank. When this is full the
wagons are brought up into which the wheat is again
transferred and then on to the elevator. The
importance of the invention is that it dispenses with
cutting and stooking, also solves the problem the
Western Farmers have experienced in getting
harvesters at the important moment. The success
has been so great it is considered it will not
be long before these machines are used universally.

Photo shows:- General view of the combined harvester
and wagon emptying the grain receptable to get it
ready for its next operation.

title: A photographic print of Home & Housing, Post War, Slums & Living Conditions (UK Wide)

date_info.rationale: Date 4/12/46 is likely 4 December 1946 given the UK format and the caption's explicit reference to 'cold weather'. April 12th is a secondary possibility.

activity: Mrs. Cropp and children at the door of their 'home', a wooden fruit picker's hut on Wested Farm.

te.text:
PROBLEM OF A WOMAN AND SIX CHILDREN
---
Living in one room - a wooden fruit picker's
hut, on Wested Farm, Crockenhill, near Swanley,
Kent, is Mrs. May Cropp, her three children and a
further three grandchildren (offspring of one of her
daughters).
She is a squatter. There is no sanitation
anywhere near the hut - nor the usual amenities. The
hut leaks, is unsanitary, and is certainly not
weather-
proof.
How she came to be there does not matter - what
does matter is that she cannot get another home to
live - and owing to the bad state of affairs the
farmer, C.T.Miller, of Wested Farm, has asked the
police to evict them in the hope that they will
be found better accomodation.
As it is, the children - ranging from a few
months to six years - cannot possibly be properly
fed, clothed and educated - and there is no talk of
them going regularly to school.
In this cold weather, some of them are to
be seen playing in the mud around their "home".
The Dartford Rural District Council, under
whose jurisdiction their "home" comes, should look
into the matter - the farmer is certainly not to
blame - it is the best housing he can offer - even
to squatters.
PICTURE SHOWS:
2. Mrs. Cropp and children at the door of their
"home".
19836   4/12/46   John Topham, Sidcup, Kent.

activity: A house at Hampton being built under a protective nylon airhouse igloo structure.

te.text:
With the compliments of British Nylon Spinners Ltd.
Press Office: 68 Knightsbridge,
London, S.W.1.
KENsington 6333
HP 118428 & HP 118431
Built up to first floor height completely in the dry, this house at
Hampton, Middlesex was the first in Britain to be protected by a nylon
airhouse. Manufactured by The Gourock Ropework Co. Ltd., the vast "igloo" of
coated nylon fabric, measuring 70 ft. by 40 ft. by 20 ft., covered the entire
site. The structure is held up solely by a constant supply of low pressure
air and experience showed that one 5,000 cubic ft./minute electric fan, costing
less than twopence an hour to run, was adequate for the greater part of the
time. Only when constant traffic was going in and out of the doors was a
second fan necessary.

te.text:
2020)   50 YEARS AS STAINED GLASS ARTIST

Mr.W.H.Jacob, of Greenfield Road, St.Helens, Lancashire,
who has just completed 50 years' service as a stained-
glass artist in the employ of Messrs.R.Seddon & Sons,
St.Helens. Mr.Jacob commenced his career as a stained-
glass artist as an apprentice at the age of 13 with his
present firm, and many specimens of his work now beauti-
fy churches and other public buildings throughout Great
Britain. He was one of the first members of the St.
Helens School of Art, and many samples of his work have
been exhibited in various parts of the country. During
his long term of office, Mr.Jacob has only once been
absent from the studios.

21/9/37.   H.   (Topical Press)

activity: A British oil-man named Lofty Sanders holding a drill-bit at an oilfield in Eakring, Nottinghamshire.

te.text: File / Industries - Fuel & Power - Oil Wells - British

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION TUESDAY'S EVENINGS, May 6th.
ENGLAND'S OILFIELD NOW PRODUCES IN MILLIONS
6.5.47.
Since 1939 England's only big-scale oilfield has produced more
than ten million gallons of oil, and the wells are now yielding
better than 150 tons a day. The field stretches for 100 square
miles beneath the "Dukeries" the name by which that area of the
English Midlands is known where so many of the premier peers have
their stately homes and family seats. This photograph was taken
at EAKRING, Nottinghamshire, where about 450 men are employed
by the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company. Oil is reached at about 2,000
feet. The typical British oil-man - LOFTY SANDERS, wearing pro-
tective headgear, holding the drill-bit which bits through the
rock and earth to reach the oil layer 2,000 feet below the ground.

THIS FILM IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

[illegible] ISSUED BY
[illegible] PHOTOS LTD.
[illegible]ations Service,
[illegible], LONDON, E.C.4

te.text:
SURVIVORS from the ill-fated oil
drilling rig Sea Gem, which col-
lapsed and sank in the North Sea
yesterday, told a story of Boxing Day
horror when they came ashore last
night.
All 32 men aboard the 5,600-ton, 10-legged rig
—which discovered a rich undersea gas field a
week ago—were plunged
into the sea when the
whole structure mys-
teriously capsized, 40
miles off Grimsby.
Late last night 20
men — some of them
injured—were known to
have survived. Three
men were picked up
dead from the icy water
and nine men were
missing.
Most of the survivors
were landed at Hull by the
2,000-ton British ship
Baltrover.
They told of the last few
minutes they spent on the
platform of the huge rig,
which was operated by
British Petroleum.

KEITH JOHNSON

LONDON [illegible]

activity: Prototype houses constructed via the 5M industrialised building system.

te.text:
CROWN COPYRIGHT RESERVED. MINISTRY OF HOUSING & LOCAL GOVERNMENT.
Four prototype houses built for the Sheffield City Council by the
Public Works Department under the 5M system of construction devised
by the Research and Development Group of the Ministry of Housing
and Local Government. This system, which marks a new attempt to
bring the advantages of industrialisation into the field of house-
building, has been derived from the 5M CLASP system used at
Stevenage for a group of old people's flatlets. The new system
is called 5M, because as at Stevenage, it is based upon a planning
grid of 1' 8" (5 x the module of 4"). The object has been to
modify the CLASP system which has been shown to have advantages in
the reduction of site labour and building time, to suit the
performance standards, and the levels of cost, of 2-storey housing.
Ministry of Housing & Local Government. January, 1963

te.text:
NOT TO BE PUBLISHED BEFORE THURSDAY'S
DAILIES 8TH FEBRUARY, 1962.

FIRST VICKERS VC 10 IS NEARING COMPLETION
ODS 7.2.62.
THE FIRST VICKERS VC 10 LONG-RANGE JET AIRLINER
IS NOW STRUCTURALLY ALMOST COMPLETE AND SYSTEM
AND FLIGHT TEST EQUIPMENT ARE BEING INSTALLED
AT THE VICKERS-ARMSTRONGS (AIRCRAFT) WORKS AT
WEYBRIDGE, SURREY. THE VC 10, THE FIRST BIG JET
AIRLINER WITH REAR-MOUNTED ENGINES, IS SCHEDULED
TO MAKE ITS FIRST FLIGHT IN MAY.
THE VC 10 IS THE BIGGEST SINGLE AIRCRAFT
PROJECT EVER TACKLED IN EUROPE. WITH ITS FOUR
ADVANCED-MODEL ROLLS-ROYCE CONWAY ENGINES IT WILL
BE THE WORLD'S MOST POWERFUL AIRLINER (ALTHOUGH
[crossed out] NOISE PROBLEMS WILL NOT BE INCREASED DUE
TO THE BETTER TAKE-OFF AND CLIMB PERFORMANCE OF THE
CLEAN-WINGED VC 10; IN FACT, IT WILL BE LESS
RESTRICTED BY AIRPORT NOISE REGULATIONS THAN CURRENT
BIG JETS). THE VC 10 CRUISES AT UP TO 600 M.P.H. ITS
MAXIMUM RANGE WITH 100 PASSENGERS AND RESERVES IS
OVER 5,000 MILES, OF 4,400 MILES WITH FULL PAY-LOAD.
ORDERS HAVE BEEN ANNOUNCED FOR 54 VC 10s -
42 FOR BOAC, FIVE FOR RAF TRANSPORT COMMAND, FOUR
FOR BRITISH UNITED AIRWAYS AND THREE FOR GHANA
AIRWAYS.
PHOTOSSHOWS:

A GENERAL VIEW SHOWING THE VICKERS VC 10
NEARING COMPLETION. THE HIGH-MOUNTED TAILPLANE
OF THE VC 10 HAS A SPAN 8FT GREATER THAN THAT OF
A SPITFIRE. E10828.

- 8 FEB 1962

te.text:
GATHERING THE NORFOLK REED HARVEST. 		AW/FM

Reed thatching in England is one of the most ancient crafts,
and the craft is reviving. The reeds come mostly from the
Norfolk Broads, where great quantities are harvested about
this time of the year, when the leaves are gone. Cutting
lasts until the young shoots appear in early April. These
reeds are used for thatching principally but are also used
for making large fish and fruit baskets, known as Skeps.

Photo shows- Gathering the reed harvest at Salhouse, Norfolk.
A flat bottomed boat laden with bundles of reeds for thatching
being pulled up-stream.
Fox Jany 27th. 37.

ROPER.   14.1.38.
BUNNY THE CART HORSE ESCAPES.
When an outdoor film sequence was made
this morning at Alexandra Palace, Bunny
the carthorse threw his rider, who was
King Marke, and escaped. The King's
knights and bodyguard chased Bunny all
over the Palace grounds and eventually
captured him, but film work was held
up for an hour. The film will be
merged into [crossed-out text] hunting scenes
to be interpolated in the television
transmission of "Tristan und Isolade",
on January 24. The actual chase seen
in this photograph will be televised
during the overture.

activity: Promotional release for Cormar Hi-Twist carpets featuring Courtaulds fibres.

te.text:
PRESS OFFICE,
22 Hanover Square,
London W.1.
TELEPHONE: MAYfair 8000

Carpets with a high twist pile are ever gaining in popularity as people
discover the advantages of a crush-resistant pile which shows no marks
of shading or scuffing. The twist in the fibre not only gives a beautiful
textured effect to a plain carpet: it also ensures that the pile is much
harder wearing.

Greenwood and Coope were the first to realise the advantages of man-made
fibres in twist pile carpets when they produced Hi-Twist, the hard twist
carpet made of 50% Courtelle/50% Evlan. This blend of Courtaulds fibres
is particularly suitable for a twist pile carpet: the thermoplastic
qualities of Courtelle mean that the twist in the pile can be set by heat,
just like the pleats in a skirt, and this twist is permanent.

Hi-Twist presents very few problems where soiling and cleaning are concerned.
The presence of Evlan in the carpet prevents any electrostatic charge
building up - it is this charge that attracts particles of dirt in acrylic
fibres. Even when normal domestic accidents occur and the carpet is stained,
it is no problem to clean because the Courtelle in the carpet means that it
shampoos beautifully and dries very quickly.

Kinky pile carpets not only look good - they also wear much better, and
so Hi-Twist, of course, qualifies for Courtaulds Extra Duty Label which
means that it can be used for any location in the home.

At 52/6d a square yard it is very good value for money.

For further information:
Miss Alexa Smith,
Ext. 347.

activity: Casting and spinning iron pipes in a British ironworks for utility services.

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION FRIDAY'S EVENINGS DECEMBER 19th.

SPINNING THE ARTERIES OF OUR CIVILISATION. 19.12.41.
This is one of a remarkable new series of photographs
taken mainly by the natural light of the processes
by which a British ironworks produce mile upon mile
of cast iron pipes for the public services of gas and
water which are prime necessity of civilised life.
A large percentage of these pipes are spun by a centrifugal
process which eliminates defects and gives a close-
grained metal, easily worked and with a high degree
of resilience and resistance to impact. In addition
to its own requirements, the plant also produces
pig-iron for steel manufacture, contributing largely
therefore to the country's output of armaments.
Blast furnace hand waiting to commence tapping.

PHOTOS. LTD.

te.text:
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
REC'D 11 AUG 1954
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

PEER TO VISIT PIT GIRLS. MJH/VIG.

In reply to a challenge by Viscount Hall, arising out of
controversy over the second reading of the Mines and Quarries
Bill in the House of Lords, the Earl of Selkirk (Paymaster
General) is to spend part of his holiday touring collieries
to "see for himself" conditions under which the "pit brow
lassies" work. Viscount Hall declared that there were about
1,000 women still employed at the pit tops working in conditions
almost as bad as those prevailing at the time, when women
were taken out of the pits nearly 100 years ago.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: 18-years-old JOAN HOLGATE, youngest member
of her shaft seen employed on the cleaning of coal at the
Bickershaw Colliery, Leigh, near Manchester. She gave up
the cleaner job of waitress to work at the pit head and is quite
happy in her work. The "pit brow lassies" work an eight-hour
shift and say that, although the work is very dirty, it is
quite congenial. A modern bath-house is provided for their
use and protective clothing is also provided.
FOX PHOTOS AUGUST 9TH. 1954. 502722.

te.text:
KING AND QUEEN TO VISIT CORNISH CLAY INDUSTRY
WILL SEE ST. AUSTELL PIT

When the King and Queen visit the West Country at the end
of October, they will inspect the china clay factory at
St. Austell, Cornwall, where the industry of china clay
digging has been carried on for 130 years.
The valuable raw material is still being mined and exported
in increasing quantities for use in drugs, cosmetics,
paper, paint, rubber and pottery making.
The white hills which surround the Lower Ninestones Pit at
St. Austell, are often spoken of as the Cornish "Alps", as a
result of the sand which is transported from the pits, and
deposited at the tops.
PHOTO SHOWS:- This joined photograph shows a clear view
of the 200 foot deep Lower Ninestones Pit, from top
to bottom.

The hosing of clay down the side of the pit can be seen
on the left, while at the bottom, are the purifying pits
and the trolleys which take the remains to the top by
railway.
MD Oct 23rd 1947 PN g

COPYRIGHT
PLANET NEWS LTD.
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
FLEET STREET, LONDON E.C.4.

25-11-57.

PRINTED CIRCUIT TRANSISTORS? TO REDUCE SIZE OF "ELECTRONIC 
BRAINS" ANNOUNCED BY DEPART OF THE U.S. ARMY.

                  Printed circuit transistors, developed
by the U.S. Army research scientist DR.J.W. LATHROP, will
greatly reduce the size of many items of military equipment
including the electronic brain of guided missile aircraft.
Use of the printed circuit method produces a transistor
about 1/20th. of an inch wide and 1,100th. of an inch high
and provides increased reliability and resistance to shock or 
vibration. It is expected that some equipment can be reduced
to one tenth of their present sizes through use of the new 
transistor to control the flow of current in electronic
circuits. Dr. Lathrop is scientist with the Army's Diamond
Fuse Laboratories, Washington, D.C.. Small "dot" on board
upper left is the new transistor, compared in size to the 
transistor presently used and a cigarette.. Photo slightly
larger than life..

activity: part of the world's largest banqueting service, ordered by the government of Ghana and completed by John Aynsley pottery firm

te.text:
PROPERTY 
 SUN 
 13 JUL 1966 
 Please return to 
 ART LIBRARY

THIS ROOMFUL of china is only part of the world's largest banqueting service. It was ordered by the government of Ghana and has just been completed by John Aynsley, a Stoke-on-Trent pottery firm. 
 Unfortunately the former president, Nkrumah, was deposed after his personal crest had been engraved on many of the pieces. The crest had to be rubbed out by the firm's craftsmen. 
 It's a good thing the service had not all been engraved; altogether there were over 18,000 pieces, from meat dishes to coffee cups. 
 The service was made in three stages. In 1960 4,800 pieces were turned out, in 1963 another 6,600 and now the last 7,000 have been completed.

te.text:
AN UNUSUAL JOB                      MJH/FM.

The unusual "line" of Mrs. Mollie Surman of Kingston
(Surrey) is making glass eyes - a very skilled craft
which she learned from her father the late Mr. G. Taylor.
Mrs. Surman, who believes she is one of the only two
women glass-eye blowers in the country, first started
to learn this craft during her school holidays at the
age of 12 and to date, she estimates that she has made
about 12,000-to 15,000 eyes.  This has been a family
craft for about 160 years. Mrs. Surman's grandfather
made glass eyes for the 2nd. Duke of Wellington, while
her father once made an artificial eye for a pedigree
Chow dog which won 1st. Prize at Crufts.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:  Blonde 38-years-old MRS. MOLLIE SURMAN
seen at work in her Kingston studio on the skilled craft
of blowing a glass eye.  It takes her about 2 hours
to make an eye.

activity: Vic Smythe supervising a string of 2-year old horses at his training grounds in Epsom.

te.text:
Esten  D.H.  3.4.44
EPSOM PREPARES FOR OPENING OF RACING SEASON
Racing opens at Windsor on Easter Monday and trainers hope that it will be the last wartime season. Victor Smythe of Epsom has 48 horses in training this year, 35 of them untried 2-year olds. The increase is mainly due to a greater allocation of feeding stuffs, but labour is still a problem. Vic Smythe solves this by being assisted by part-time local labour to assist in riding and gallops. One of these is an Irish nurse from a local hospital who rides the horses in gallops with as much nerve as her professional colleagues.
OPS 1 Vic Smythe (on left) supervises a string consisting of 2-year olds.  He hopes the Derby will be run on his home ground next year.

activity: A team of international testers assessing a gas strike at a gas well in a field on a farm in South Godstone.

te.text:
ARTHUR STEEL SUN 3.1.66 
In a field at South Godstone a gas well and a team of testers. 
O.P.S. L. to R... Jean Cros (Beziers), Phillipe Neyron (Beziers), John 
Trewhella (Cornwall) Chief, Ken Atwood (Houston, Texas) engineer from Esso, 
and Jan Groenestein from Amsterdam.

FARMER John Collard tended his
cattle and sheep as usual yester-
day. He was philosophical about
the men ploughing through the
mud in his bottom field—even
though they have struck gas.
Said Mr. Collard: "It won't make
much difference to me even if large
quantities of the gas are found."
He's right, too. For in Britain all
mineral rights are vested in the Crown
(which means, in this case, the Ministry
of Power).
The prospectors, too, were philo-
sophical about their strike on the
Collards' 200-acre farm at South
Godstone, Surrey.
Cornishman John Trewhella, who now
lives at Alkmaar in Holland, said:
"Optimistic? That's too strong a word.
We're just hopeful."
Mr. Trewhella, who
heads the team of con-
tractors called in to assess
the quality and quantity
of the strike, said: "We
will be testing for a week
or 10 days. Then we
should know how much
gas is here."
STRIKE
The search for gas down
on the farm began long
before the North Sea hunt.
The Esso Petroleum Com-
pany were granted prospect-
ing licences six years ago.
They negotiated agreements
with landowners in Hampshire,
Sussex, Kent and Surrey—and
began drilling four years ago.
From Mr. Collard they rented
a field on Langham Park Farm
where villagers had played foot-
ball for nearly 40 years.
And it was there that Esso
scored with an international
team captained by 37-year-old
Ken Atwood, of Houston, Texas.
Working with him and Mr.
Trewhella are Dutch and
French drilling experts.
Their strike is just off the
main London-Eastbourne road
—23 miles from London—oppo-
site Gus Rossini's transport
café.
GUSHER
Mr. Rossini said last night:
"When the gas is gushing, it's
lit. And the flames reach 30ft.
high or more. Then it's like a
fairground round here."
Friends who don't know about
mineral rights optimistically tell
Farmer Collard: "You'll be a
millionaire..."
But with an appropriate agri-
cultural turn of phrase, Mr.
Collard commented: "They're
counting my chickens before
they are hatched."
Brightening, he added: "We
must get a private pipeline.
After all, we cook with gas."
Industry.. Fuel and Power.. Gas wells in Surrey

BRITISH OFFICIAL PHOTOGRAPH NO. T.29 (WN).
MINISTRY OF FUEL AND POWER) CROWN COPYRIGHT
RESERVED
OPERATION PLUTO (PIPE LINES UNDER THE OCEAN)
FIRST PICTURES.
One of the greatest supply stories of the war is now
being told for the first time. It is the story of
Operation "Pluto" (from the initial letters of
"Pipe Lines Under The Ocean") It tells of the laying
by unique methods of an oil pipe line system under
the Englsih Channel by which the Miliarty operations
of the Allied Armies in Europe were noursshed. This
system was devised by the Petroleum Warfare Dept.
and its success owes much to the Prime Minister's
interest.
(These photo shows tie up with the Ministry of
Fuel and Power Press Conference on Tuesday May 22nd.
Picture shows. Drums for carrying steel pipe were
known as "Conuns" (H.M.S. Conundrums). This picture
shows a Conun being towed by the Royal Navy across
the Channel and laying the first continuous length
of stee pipe 67 miles long.

MUST NOT BE PUBLISHED BEFORE 00.30. HOURS THURSDAY
MAY 24th. I.E. FOR THURSDAY MORNING PAPERS.

SET OF APOSTLE SPOONS OFFERED FOR SALE-AT CHRISTIES
BOUGHT-IN AT £6,200..

           A complete set of very rare
Elizabethan Apostle Spoons - property of MR. JAMES
MABON of New York - were offered for sale at Christies
this morning - and were 'bought in' for £6,200. The
spoons - known as the 'Frith Set' - because they
were once owned by the Victorian Squire Frith of

an 'Apostle' set - one for each apostle and on e

bear the hallmark 1592 - the thirteenth spoon is
somewhat later.

FOR WEDNESDAY'S DAILIES

JS. 10.12.52.
Now nearing completion in readiness for the launching
ceremony on December 17th at Messrs John Brown's shipyard
on the Clyde, is the 32,000-ton tanker "BRITISH SAILOR"
the first of seven similar sized tankers for the British
Tanker Company. The vessel will be the largest oil tanker
ever launched on the Clyde, and will be the largest British
owned tanker sailing the seas. Nearby in the same yard a
start has been made on the second tanker, the "BRITISH
SOLDIER" and they will make a valuable addition to the
British Tanker Company's fleet bringing oil from the Middle
East to the refineries in Britain. This is one of a series
taken illustrating their construction, and shows:-

te.text:
THE ROYAL SHOW  1963.                PC/

The Royal Show 1963 is taking place at
Stoneleigh Abbey Park, near Kenilworth,
Warwickshire.  For nearly one hundred
and twenty five years the Royal Show has
been taking place annually in various
parts of the country - it has now returned
to the Midlands to Stoneleigh Abbey, the
seat of Lord Leigh, which is hoped will
become its permanent site.  During the
many years the show has been taking place,
a great deal of changes have been made
to its presentation - and this years new
feature is the helicopter service from
which visitors can get an overall view
of the enormous area covered by the show
rings and exhibition stands. During the
build-up for the show the extremely bad
and wet weather has caused much havoc
but thanks to the herculean efforts made
by all concerned the show will go on as
usual. H.M.Queen Elizabeth II and the
Duke of Edinburgh, (President of the Royal
Agricultural Society of England this year)
will visit the show on Thursday, 4th. They
are expected to enter the main ring in a
carriage drawn by Windsor Greys.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:-   An aerial view of
the Royal Show, at Stoneleigh Abbey Park,
Warwickshire, to-day, Monday.

FIRST DROPS OF A NEW WINE
Nov 14th 1956 PAR 60018-1 (Wo-J)


FIRST DROPS OF A NEW WINE

Assistant 'vigneron' ERNEST BLACKMAN holds a
jug to catch the first drops being squeezed
from the press by Sir GUY SALISBURY-JONES,
Marshal of the Diplomatic Corps, pressing
grapes for a new wine at his country home at
Hambledon, Hampshire.
Watching are LADY SALISBURY-JONES, their son
RAYMOND and daughter MARIETTE.
The wine, to be named 'Hambledon', will be
matured by next July and placed on the market
in time for Christmas next year.
The vineyard at Hambledon is in its fifth year
but grapes from younger vines are not good
enough for wine.  Sir Guy bottled some of
last year's crop for his own use this
Christmas but it will not be sold.
Despite bad weather this year, the grapes have
exceeded expectations at Hambledon and are in
better condition than those at many of the
famous French vineyards.
Nov 14th 1956 PAR 60018-1 (Wo-J)

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN EVENING PAPERS OF

activity: squaring through a length of netting with a knife

te.text:
THE MODERN GIRL PLIES A CENTURIES-OLD TRADE
July 13th 1953 PAR 36404 -2 (BKS-R)
_________________________________________________________
THE MODERN GIRL PLIES A CENTURIES-OLD TRADE

For at least seven centuries, the manufacture
of nets, ropes, sailcloth and other hempen
products has been the staple industry of
the town of Bridport, Dorset.
Of Bridport's present-day population of about
6,000, over a thousand - many of them young
women - are engaged in the industry,
directly or indirectly.
At one time locally-grown flax and hemp were
used, but nearly all the raw material is
now imported.
It is recorded that all the ropes and sails
for King John's Navy (he reigned from
1199-1216) were made at Bridport. And the
expression 'stabbed by a Bridport dagger' for
a person who had been hanged was current
in 1530, when King Henry VIII reigned.
This picture was taken in the Bridport works
of Joseph Gundry and Co. Ltd., a firm founded
in 1665 and still controlled by lineal
descendants of the founder. There were
Gundrys engaged in the trade as early as 1580.
PICTURE SHOWS:- PHYLLIS STROUD, attractive
representative of modern Bridport,
'squaring through' a length of netting
with a knife.
July 13th 1953 PAR 36404-2 (BKS-R)

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN EVENING
PAPERS OF TUESDAY, JULY 14th.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
RCD. 15 JUL 1953

activity: 70 year old blacksmith Nathaniel Barber at his forge at Milford Mill

te.text:
ESTEN    D.H.    1.2.44.
NAT'S SCORE IS 25,000 not out.
In the tiny hamlet of Milford situated on the
outskirts of Salisbury lives 70 year old Nathaniel
Barber, Blacksmith for 53 years. Nat belongs to
a fast dying profession, for blacksmiths are now
becoming a rarity.
Motor Engineer is the new term for where Nat used
to shoe over 200 horses six times a year, now only
20 come to him to be reshod.
Nat's father was a blacksmith as were four of his
eight brothers of whom he is the only one left.
In spite of the lack of horses to shoe, Nat
persuaded his 40 year old son to learn the craft
and now when Nat passes on, Ronald will become the
fourth generation of Barber - Blacksmith.
Nat boasts of the time he shood famous racehorses
in the district.
Nat estimates that he has made and forged 25,000
shoes in his 53 years and hopes to make a few more
thousand yet. He works from dawn till dusk six
days a week throughout the year.
There is another son, Horace, profession motor
engineer.
O.P.S.1    70 year old Nat. Barber at the forge
           at Milford Mill.

activity: Elizabeth Greenhill bookbinding in her Essex Street workshop.

te.text:
ANCIENT CRAFT IN MODERN LONDON.
WOMAN BOOKBINDER WORKS ON HISTORIC SITE.

An ancient handicraft is being carried
on in a basement in Essex Street, within
earshot of the bustling Strand, by
Miss Elizabeth Greenhill, the bookbinder.
Miss Greenhill has opened a new workshop
in the house which used to be the old
water-gate to Essex House in the days when
it was the palace of Robert Devereux,
Earl of Essex, and favourite of Queen
Elizabeth.
Miss Greenhill first achieved fame in her
craft when she bound "The Gloucester Bible",
the personal gift of Mr. Leslie Boyce, M.P.
to Gloucester City to commemorate the
jubilee of King George V.
She has just completed a special binding
for a copy of "Pride and Prejudice" for
Queen Mary, and another book for Princess
Margaret Rose.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Miss Elizabeth Greenhill busy
in her workshop at the foot of Essex Stairs,
Essex Street.
GAIC September 29th 1937 PN-r.

COPYRIGHT.
PLANET NEWS LTD
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON, E.C. 4.

SUSSEX BUILDING CONTRACTOR BEATS THE WEATHER.

of WARNHAM VILLAGE, near Horsham, Sussex has put
into practice an idea which he thinks will soon
sweep the country .. He has put his building sites

breaks - on a three bedroomed house at the L.C.C.s

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN DAILIES
OF FRIDAY 9TH OCTOBER 1964.

NORTH SEA GEOPHYSICAL OPERATIONS.
ERF. G. OCTOBER 1964
BRITISH PETROLEUM HAS BEEN AWARDED PRODUCTION
LICENCES BY THE MINISTRY OF POWER, COVERING
SOME 2,200 SQUARE MILES IN AREA, TO SEARCH FOR
AND PRODUCE OIL AND NATURAL GAS UNDER THE
NORTH SEA ADJACENT TO THE UNITED KINGDOM. THE
AREAS LIE OFF THE COAST OF DURHAM, YORKSHIRE
AND LINCOLNSHIRE.
THE COMPANY HAS DRAWN UP PLANS FOR
ITS OWN SUBSTANTIAL DRILLING PROGRAMME. THE
B.P. AREA HAS BEEN DIVIDED INTO THREE PRODUCTION
LICENCES, IN EACH OF WHICH ONE DEEP TEST WILL
INITIALLY BE DRILLED; THE PROGRAMME FOR FURTHER
TEST DRILLING WILL BE DRAWN UP AS DICTATED BY
EXPERIENCED IT IS EXPECTED THAT EACH WELL WILL BE
ABOUT 12,000 FEET IN DEPTH AND WILL COST AT LEAST
£500,000. DRILLING OPERATIONS WILL COMMENCE
AS EARLY AS PRACTICABLE IN 1965. GEOPHYSICAL
WORK HAS ALREADY BEGUN IN ORDER TO AID SELECTION
OF DRILLING LOCATIONS.
PHOTO SHOWS:
ON BOARD THE SURVEY VESSEL "TEXIN" - SIGNALS
FROM EACH SHOCK WAVE, WHICH APART FROM BEING
RECORDED ON TAPE, ( [illegible] ), ARE PHOTOGRAPHICALLY
REPRODUCED AS AN IMMEDIATE VISUAL CHECK.
THE EFFECT OF THE SHOCK WAVES ARE RELAYED BY THE
"STREAMER" FROM THE DEPTH CHARGES ECHOED FROM
THE ROCK FORMATION BELOW THE SEA BED.
THE "STREAMER" IS RUN OUT ASTERN
OF THE SHIP AND IS SOMETIMES WELL OVER A MILE
LONG.
G.10014

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY'S EVENINGS, Oct 2nd.

SEA PLANES WILL SEEK WHALES FOR FLOATING FACTORY
                                          2.10.46.
The United Whalers' 15000-ton factory ship BALAENA, first of
its kind to be fitted with aircraft for whale-spotting and
weather reconnaissance, has been handed over to her owners
after trials in Belfast Lough, and will shortly leave for
the Antarctic in search of badly needed whale oil.
The ship will carry three converted Walrus amphibian air-
craft which will be launched from a double-acting catapult
working on a cordite charge, or lowered over the side for a
normal take-off by the crane which also lifts them from the
water after a flight.
The BALAENA will act as mother ship for a fleet of about ten
whale-catchers, and her factory contains one of the largest
oil-producing plants ever installed in a ship, and elaborate
machinery for dealing with by-products; refrigerating gear
will freeze the choicest parts of the whale meat for human
consumption.   The picture shows

BALAENA, showing one of the amphibian Walruses and the

hauled up into the factory.

te.text:
DAILY HERALD ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

1,000,000, EELS.
LIVE IN A BARGE FULL OF HOLES          DG/FM

Believed to be the first of its kind ever to
be built in this country, and certainly the
first of this particular design, the eel barge
"Johan", is literally a ship full of holes.
The centre part of the barge is perforated so that
water can be allowed to flow freely into it.
Watertight compartments support the barge, fore and
aft, and the deck is no more than 18 inches above
water level. The owner is Mr H. G. Kuitjen,
an importer of live eels. The eels come from
the seas between Norway and Corsica, and they are
brought by boat from the Continent.
The eels usually arrive in the autumn and are
graded by size into separate compartments. From
the barge they are packed into wet boxes for
Billingsgate. It is estimated that the barge
will 120,000 lbs of live eels- the shipping of
this 50 ton cargo will not increase the draught
draught of the vessel as the cargo is waterborne.

PHOTO SHOWS:- The graded eels are transferred into
floating containers alongside the barge at Heybridge
Basin, Malden, Essex. These are also floating
perforated containers.

activity: Profile of a retired farm horse named Old Captain used for horse-hoeing sugar-beet.

te.text:
THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

Goodbye,
old friend!
WHEN summer comes, and
the green rows of sugar-
beet glisten in the sun,
we shall miss Old Captain.
For it has been Sam's custom
for many years, on mornings when
butterflies have danced and the
cuckoo's call has sounded over the
fields, to go into the stable and
say to the boy George: "Horse-
hoeing—we'll take Captain."
He was the obvious choice. No
other horse could do it so well.
Ever since he was first broken-in
as a colt, horse-hoeing has been
his job on the farm.
It meant walking steadily and
carefully between the rows, up and
down the field, up and down, hour
after hour, in the heat of the sun.
It was irksome, monotonous work.
But it was work that, done well,
added tons to the crop.
Captain—the willing horse—did
it always. And in the intervals
between one long horse-hoeing
season and another he did odd
jobs of carting mangolds and
muck and straw and water with a
stolid patience that earned him
the reputation of being the most
reliable old plodder we have ever
had on this farm.
"He was a kind ole hoss," says
Sam.

OLD Captain stands motion-
less in the horseyard, with
his head lowered almost to
his knees, a living symbol of
that greatest of farming vir-
tues, patience.

te.text:
THEY SWEAT FOR BRITAIN. 				E.M./RS.

Men now working in the great foundries of the Ministry of
Supply are going at overpowering pressure to supply, not
only our Army with all the modern weapons to beat the 'Hun',
but more and more tanks and guns for Russia.  Before going
into these great factories, many of the men were clerks,
motor-drivers, horse dealers, roundsmen, etc., jobs which
are far removed from their present employment, but, as can
be seen from these pictures, this is no handicap to them
and they are putting every effort into their new tasks.

Photo shows:-  Mr. Woolston, who, before the war was a
heavy timber carrier, makes light work of his new job
and enjoys the joke as he wrings the sweat from his vest
after a day's work.
FOX.  9th October, 1941.				263518.

CERTIFIED 
FOR PUBLICATION 
AS PASSED BY 
PRESS AND CENSOR BUREAU

activity: Mr Leslie Payne, General Manager of H.A. Tidnam wine company, emerging from subterranean wine vaults in Wisbech

te.text:
"LOOK WHAT I'VE FOUND" 					DG/VIG
THE XMAS SPIRIT BENEATH THE TOWN

Mr. LESLIE PAYNE, of Wisbech, seems to have made a
startling (and very seasonable) find under the
signpost directing folks to Kings Lynn and Peterborough.
The truth is, however, that Mr Payne, is the General
Manager of the old established wine company of
H.A. Tidnam, Wisbech, and he is emerging from the
company's vaults - once secret passages beneath the town.
Passage - which is crammed full of Christmas wine -
once ran from William the Conqueror's Wisbech castle
to the edge of the castle grounds. Gunpowder plotters
Catesby and Tresham, were once imprisoned in the vaults.

activity: building a 24 ft. yacht in a back garden

te.text:
BACK-YARD BOAT-BUILDERS PLAN TO SAIL TO AUSTRALIA D/HA

Neighbours of Mr and Mrs P.J. Munro of Oxberry Avenue,
Fulham, can seen ship-building in progress from their
back windows. Mr. Munro, production manager of cosmetics
with a West End hairdresser, is at present building a
24 ft. yacht in the back garden, assisted by building
worker, Mr. H. Woodbridge, and he and his wife hope to
sail to Australia. Their only experience of sailing so
far has been on the Norfolk Broads, and Mr. Munro has
been building the £500 boat from library books. When
finished the craft will be lifted into the lane at the
back, and taken to Putney where it will be launched,
it is hoped this summer.

PHOTO SHOWS: Mr. P.J. Munro (in beret) and Mr. H.
Woodbridge, photographed at work on the 24 ft. yacht
in the back garden at Oxberry Avenue.

FOX PHOTOS 459353 16th Jan., 1952

'SATURDAY NIGHT OUT' WITH THE 'LOWESTOFT LADY'

The 100-foot trawler 'LOWESTOFT LADY', 
from which viewers of the BBC's 
'Saturday Night Out' programme will 
see the herring fleet on the fishing

transmitting pictures from the trawler

activity: Mrs. May Cropp with her three children and grandchildren in their one-roomed wooden fruit picker's hut on Wested Farm.

te.text:
PROBLEM OF A WOMAN AND SIX CHILDREN
---
Living in one room - a wooden fruit picker's
hut, on Wested Farm, Crockenhill, near Swanley,
Kent, is Mrs. May Cropp, her three children and a
further three granchildren (offspring of one of her
daughters).
She is a squatter. There is no sanitation
anywhere near the hut - nor the usual amenities. The
hut leaks, is unsanitary, and is certainly not
weatherproof.
How she came to be there does not matter - what
does matter is that she cannot get another home to
live - and owing to the bad state of affairs the
farmer, C.T. Miller, of Wested Farm, has asked the
police to evict them in the hope that they will
be found better accomodation.
As it is, the children - ranging from a few
months to six years - cannot possibly be properly
fed, clothed and educated - and there is no talk of
them going regularly to school.
In this cold weather, some of them are to
be seen playing in the mud around their "home".
The Dartford Rural District Council, under
whose jurisdiction their "home" comes, should look
into the matter - the farmer is certainly not to
blame - it is the best housing he can offer - even
to squatters.
PICTURE SHOWS:

1. Mrs. May Cropp with her three children
and granchildren in their one roomed hut.

19835 4/12/46 John Topham, Sidcup, Kent.

Fil Housing P.W. Slums.
XR Dartford
XR Personal

activity: fellers felling a pine tree in Rendlesham Forest

te.text:
BUILDING UP OUR TIMBER STOCKS.        MJH/HT

During the two World Wars, our woodlands were
seriously denuded of timber. Today, the Forestry
Commission and private woodland owners are pressing
ahead with the vital task of forming new forests and
re-stocking the old. The year 1956 has marked a milestone
in the history of the Forestry Commission, for it has
seen the planting by the Commission of the one
millionth acre of new woodland. Thus the area of woodland
planted to date by the Commission is more than 1,500
square miles - an area larger than Kent, nearly
twice the extent of Glamorgan and nearly two-thirds
of Perthshire. This million acres is made up of some
500 forests, which are well distributed over the length
and breadth of Britain. In recent years, well over
100-million trees - including more than 10 million hardwoods -
have been planted annually by the Commission and many of
the forests are now producing timber in substantial
quantities; in 1955, the total production amounted to
600,000 tons. Today there is hardly a county without
a national forest and scenes such as these, in the
Commission's Rendlesham Forest in East Anglia, are typical
of what is to be seen in many other parts of the country.


PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: "Timber" and the fellers
crouch as a pine comes crashing down in
Rendlesham Forest (Suffolk).
FOX PHOTOS AUGUST 23RD. 1956        547150.

is big enough to be put with "Moina".

activity: the use of pre-cast concrete embrasures for rapidly constructed sandbagged blockhouses

te.text:
EMBRASURES FOR SANDBAGGED BUILT BLOCKHOUSES.
The weak feature in all rapidly constructed blockhouses
is the wooden framing used to form the opening.  The
opening does not protect the rifleman because the rim
can be penetrated by a bullet, also the splintered wood
carried away by the bullet can produce nasty wounds.
The present suggestion is to pre-cast the embrasure
opening of the desired aperture and angle, the outer
extremity having a light sheet steel framing embedded
in the face to prevent the concrete edges shattered by
a bullet from being detached and forming missiles.
The embrasure weighs less than 1½ cwt. and can easily
be lifted into place by two men.  Manufacture can be
made in quite simple wooden moulds by any local building
contractor, breeze block manufacturer, in Corporation
yards, and so on; using the quick setting concrete
and be produced ready for installation within 24 hours.

activity: wives waiting at the pit-head for news during the Auchengeich Colliery disaster

te.text:
THE pit where 45 men
are trapped behind a
wall of flame became an
almost-certain grave last
night. Rescuers had
found a pocket of deadly
carbon monoxide gas
spreading through the
shaft where the men were
caught.
The gas—miners call it
"White Damp"—is caused
by the fire as it rages through
the pit workings at Auchen-
geich Colliery, at Chryston,
near Glasgow.
It can kill in a short time.
The men were trapped in the
shaft as they rode from the pit
bottom to the coal face on a
bogie train.
Heavy
Last night, more than 12
hours after the outbreak, res-
cuers were still trying to reach
the train in a haulage way,
1,050 feet down.
One of them said as he came
to the surface: "Anyone in that
part of the haulage way is dead.
"The whole place is alight,
glowing red and as hot as a coke
oven. Every scrap of timber is
on fire. Identification of many
of the bodies may be very
difficult."
And a Coal Board statement
said: "It is feared that a heavy
loss of life must be expected."

te.text:
PROPERTY
4 JUN 1969
please return to
ART LIBRARY

MEN WITHOUT NERVES
June 3rd 1969 PAP 140039-3 (M-G)

MEN WITHOUT NERVES

Some 500 ft. above the Severn, HENRI DONALD of
Aberdeen (top), GERRY CALLOWAY of Blandford
(centre) and GEOFF CHARLTON of Weymouth
nervelessly work on a "spacer" that runs
along the pilot cable when replacing power
lines over the river at Aust,
Gloucestershire.
A team of 25 men from the J.L. Eve
Construction Co., Ltd., is replacing seven
cables, each weighing 28 1/2 tons and each
2 1/2 miles of steel cord with aluminium
covering. The new power lines are aerodynamic
in section to prevent wind trouble experienced
when the old lines swung in the wind
and touched in the centre. This caused
arcing.
Re-wiring the 275 kilovolt double circuit
crossing is expected to take up to five months.
The work is being carried out for the Central
Electricity Generating Board.
June 3rd 1969 PAP 140039-3 (M-G)

PRESS ASSOCIATION PHOTOS

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN EVENING PAPERS
OF TUESDAY, JUNE 3rd

te.text:
Malindine.        ILL.        13/2/46
Bread.
Government Vocational Training Scheme "Baking
Course" at Brighton Technical College.
Bakery is among the large variety of skilled
manual trades, for which courses of training are
now available, for men and womenx now being released
from War Service. The courses of six months
duration and upwards, according to trade chosen
by trainees, are given either at, Government
Training Centres, or Technical Colleges, or
completely by employers. During training period
all trainees receive allowances, free of income
tax, on completion of training the Ministry of
Labour assists in finding jobs, up to the
qualifications gained by the trainees.
At the [crossed out] Brighton Technical College, on the
28th January, a former A.T.S. Cook Sgt. aP/Lt.
and ten other Ex Servicemen began a 17 week
bakery course. Under the instructions of Mr. L.O.
Smith a former, United Kingdom National Diploma
winner, who until Jan, was a Warrant Officer Master
Baker instructor, in the Army, now demobilies,
he hopes to pass on much of his experience to
ex service colleagues.
Ops. 1.
Types of Bread Baked by the Trainees during there
course at the Brighton Technical College.

MAY 22nd. 1969.

PRESERVATION WORK ON WORLD'S OLDEST WOODEN CHURCH.

Work to deal with death watch beetle, wood rot,
etc, is being carried out at the little church of St.
Andrew's Greensted, near Ongar, Essex, believed to be
the oldest wooden church in the world.  The church is
unique, dating from 845 A.D. - with 1,000 year old wooden
walls of cleft tree trunks.   The preservation work
is being carried out by Rentokil.

KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS: 2-   ALAN RUFFEL, of Rentokil,
been at work on the 1,000 year old wooden walls,
of the ancient church.  He is using an injection
gun.
H/Keystone   JG/818568

KEYSTONE

te.text:
The egg and
Biddy
Herald Reporter
PENZANCE, Friday.
THE egg that Biddy the hen
laid today made farmer's
wife Mrs. Jane North think:
What next?
For Biddy has been playing some
queer tricks in the last few days
at Trungle Farm, Paul, near
here.
EGG 1 a few days ago made Mrs.
North Happy—it was fit for son
George's breakfast.
EGG 2 the next day was so small
it made her wonder if a ban-
tam had strayed among her
hens.
EGG 3 the following day was the
smallest ever known in the dis-
trict.
EGG 4 today crowned them all:
it was oblong with a tube ar-
rangement at one end.
Herald poultry expert Alan
Thompson says Biddy probably
has an ailment which affects
the shell-making "mechanism."

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY'S EVENINGS, June 25th.
PROGRESS ON BRITAIN'S AERIAL GIANT
25.6.47.
At the Bristol Aeroplane Works at FILTON, progress is being
made on the huge 125-ton "Brabazon I" landplane - the largest
ever to be built in Britain - which when completed will carry
100 people direct from London to New York. A special runway,
for which a complete village had to be demolished and which
will cost £2,000,000, and an assembly hall, are being con-
structed to get this giant into the air. She will have a wing-
span of 230 ft (30ft longer than between the main structures
of Tower Bridge), and will be powered by eight Centaurus gas-
turbines of 2500 h.p. each. The picture shows -
A general view of the huge machine under construction in the
Bristol workshops. The giant fuselage and centre sections of
the wings are supported by cradles and scaffolding, while in the
foreground one of the massive outer wings is being erected.
The aircraft is being constructed in portions, which will
later be moved to the giant assembly hall for the final
assembly.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED

COPYRIGHT PHOTO ISSUED BY,
CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
INCORPORATING

activity: Sale of the Marshall traction engine 'Prince Andrew' with operators Michael and W.B. Dawson.

te.text:
KT/B58.
"PRINCE ANDREW" BEING SOLD.
Built in 1914, the 7 Horse Power Marshall general
purpose traction engine "PRINCE ANDREW" is well-known to
Lincolnshire farmers who have used it for threshing.
It was owned by a contractor until 1957 when it was
bought by Geo.R.Dawson & Sons of Bicker, Boston, Lincs.
Now as it is surplus to that firm's requirements, it is
to be sold by auction, along with three other traction
engines. "Prince Andrew" is a favourite of 14-year-old
MICHAEL DAWSON who has driven it in rallies for the past
three years. The engine has won numerous prizes at rallies
throughout the country including the cup for the Best
Preserved Traction Engine at a National Rally held in
London.
PHOTO SHOWS.
Traction engine PRINCE ANDREW with it's
young driver MICHAEL DAWSON (right), his uncle
W.B.DAWSON (left), and W.B.DAWSON Junior.
FOX PHOTOS    20th JULY 1964.    3.

BY
FOX PHOTOS LTD.

HORACE IS A MODEL AIRMAN.		AW/HT

The Ministry of Supply have made a scientifically
worked-out model airman for use by plane designers.
Already nicknamed " Horace ", this average airman is
hinged in eight places, and is being used at Farnborough,
Hants, " to establish a standard to which various
dimensional and strength requirements associated with
aircrew positions can be related ".  Dressed for his
test, Horace weighs 200 lbs, and is over 6 ft tall; he
is as much as two men can manage.

Photo shows - " Horace " is fired in an ejector seat
on a special tower to test equipment during experiments
at Farnborough.  The smoke comes from the cordite
cartridges used to throw him up.
Fox April 9th, 48.

activity: 92-year-old hurdle-maker William Howell at work in his Gloucestershire workshop.

te.text:
BUSY HURDLE MAKER - AT NEARLY 92.

At nearly 92 years of age MR. WILLIAM
HOWELL is still one of the busiest hurdle-makers
in sheep farming Gloucestershire. This year
he supplied sheep hurdles for the Royal, the Welsh
Royal, the Bath and West, and the Three Counties
Agricultural Shows. With his 60-year old son,
Charles, Mr. Howell still works a 7-hour day. His
spare time hobby is composing poetry. He has never
written any down but recently his family have made
tape recordings of his poems. Mr. Howell's
workshop is in Church Street, Moreton-in-the-Marsh,
Gloucestershire and people who see him working there
tell him he doesn't look a day over 70.

te.text:
23. 1. 56.

MAKING NEW RIGGING FOR NELSON'S FLAGSHIP "VICTORY"

A team of men and women have started work at Chatham 
to make a complete new rigging for Nelson's Flagship, 
VICTORY". They are working in the same timber-built 
rope "walks" used by the men who refitted Victory for 
Trafalgar after she had been for five years in the 
Medway as a prison hospital ship. The work is being 
carried out at Chatham's Ropery - the Admiralty's only 
rope-making establishment. Methods of making the rope 
are almost the same as in the days of Nelson except 
that women are employed in some of the operations, 
now done by machines.
PHOTO SHOWS        MRS LILIAN McBRIDE keeping control
                   of the thinner machine which is
                   spinning the thread from sisal cans
                   for the use of the rope makers in 
                   the rope "walk" which is 1,128 feet 
                   in length.
EM/J.              Keystone.         EM/651127.

PROPERTY OF 
DAILY HERALD

24 JAN 1956

PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

activity: hand-making cricket balls in a factory

te.text:
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
17 JAN 1962
RETURN
ART LIBRARY

On the ball as usual—Craftsman Ken Jeffrey
Strike? They’ll all
play it straight
A STEADY stitcher is
this chap, 50-year-old
Ken Jeffrey. And yester-
day he stitched on as care-
fully as usual—unworried
by the dispute in his little
industry.
He is one of the men
demanding a pay rise for
their very special craft—
making cricket balls by
hand.
The men are expected to
stage Britain's friendliest
walk-out in nine days.
Employees and workers
are prepared for a long
spell of stone-walling.
Both sides are determined
that the affair—their first
major wage disagreement
in 30 years—should be
managed cordially.
NO CHANGE
In the smal family firms
—all in Kent—that make
up the country's cricket-
ball industry the works
manager is just "one of
the chaps." And no-one is
quite sure about strike
rules anyway.
Eight-five ball makers at
three Tonbridge firms and
35 at Teston, near Maid-
stone, are involved. So are
36 bat makers at Roberts-
bridge, Sussex.
They want a rise which
would add about 25s. a
week to their pay packets,
which range from £9 to
£16.
At the two-storey
Lillywhite Frowd factory
at Tonbridge, works man-
ager John Dyer said
yesterday: "We’re a happy
bunch here and the strike
won’t change a thing."
"If the chaps do walk
out I'll be drinking in the
pub with them just the
same."
'KNOCK 'EM'
But he added: "I don't
agree with them. A pay
rise would kill the industry
with the cut price compe-
tition from machine-made
cricket balls from Aus-
tralia, Pakistan and
India."
Mr. Roy Thomas, branch
secretary of the National
Union of Furniture Trade
Operatives (Cricket Ball
Section) works at the fac-
tory as a closer—shaping
cricket ball covers.
"We'll knock them for
six," he said. "We’re badly
done by compared with
workers in other indus-
tries.
"But there will be no
animosity. We can get
through this spot of bother
without falling out."

te.text:
INSPECTION OF THE PROGRESS MADE IN THE
CONSTRUCTION OF THE WORLD'S LARGEST FLYING-BOATS. 26-7-49.

Excellent progress is being made with the three Saunders -
Roe, Princess class, 140-ton flying-boats, known as the
S.R.45, and the largest flying-boats in the world, at the
ship-yards at Cowes, Isle of Wight. The 10-engined
aircraft are expected to be delivered to B.O.A.C. on
schedule - the first before the end of 1950, and the
others during 1951. The aircraft will be able to carry
between 80 and 100 passengers - and will have an effective
range of 5,500 miles, sufficient to maintain non-stop
services between Southampton and New York. They will be
powered by Bristol Proteus airscrew-turbine engines..
KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:- A team of workmen working a
hawser which moves the 30-ton hull at 3ins. a

hangar....

te.text:
IRELAND.						FH/LAL.

A UNIQUE AND PICTURESQUE SIGHT.

These pictures show linen bleaching at Banbridge. Co., Down.
The water of the River Ban is unique as it is more suitable
for the manufacture of linen than any other water in the world.
Various scientists have made extensive tests to discover what
makes the Ban water linen-conscious, but have failed. Ninety
per cent of Irish linen has been woven and bleached on the banks
of the Ban and probably 50% of it was made at Banbridge. It is
a picturesque and unique sight to see the linen in the fields.

...shows - The picturesque and unique sight of linen laid
...leaching in the fields of Banbridge.
...9th. 34

te.text:
The beer drain,
hitting Britain

HALF A MILLION pints went down the drain
yesterday. Half a million pints that 1,500 Midland
pubs and clubs would have welcomed in their fast-
dwindling cellars. Half a million pints on which the
Government would have been glad to collect £25,000
excise duty. Half a million pints that Ansells
Brewery in Birmingham have had to write off
because 1,000 of their workers have been on strike
for three days. All that is holding up a return to
work is the pay the men's union are demanding for
seven men, suspended in a dispute over a non-
union worker. Just £40.

SU. AGENT.   16-2-68.   R. Williams.
And not a drop to drink. At Ansell's Brewery ston Bham 
as 500,000
pints go down the drain.

PROPERTY
OF

activity: Ivor Jones pulling an electrically driven delivery van from Leicester to London.

te.text:
FROM LEICESTER TO LONDON -- PULLING
ELECRICALLY DRIVEN DELIVERY VAN.

IVOR JONES, 24, of Leicester, believed
he was the most unique of Saturday's walkers.
He set out from Leicester at 1.30 p.m. on Friday
pulling an electrically driven delivery van. Twenty-
four hours later he was at [crossed out] Markyate, near
Dunstable, 30 miles from his objective, Marble Arch.
"This is the first and last time I shall do anything
like this and I am only doing it now because a friend
bet me a fiver I couldn't make it", he said. Ivor,
who was listening to the efforts of the other walkers
on a radio strapped to the top of the van, added:
"I know this will not be any record time but I can't
go any faster as every 17 miles I have to stop for
half-an-hour while the van's batteries are re-charged.
"I have had no training, but so far I've not got any
blisters. My only discomforture is that I have
caught a cold".
KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:- IVOR JONES pictured
passing through Dunstable today.
R Keystone 1856/711158

KEYSTONE PRESS AGENCY LTD.
4-7 RED LION COURT,
FLEET ST. LONDON, E.C.4

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION SATURDAY'S DAILIES MAY 23rd

GIRLS MAKE STEEL FOR TANKS AND SHIPS.
22.5.42.
When the Ministry of Supply decided to open a new
steel foundry in Scotland to meet the demands for
tanks for Russia and plates for ship repairs, it
was discovered that there were not enough men at
hand to work it. Local women and girls, therefore
determined that the running of the new foundry
should be their special war effort, with the result
that they are now doing everything there except the
actual smelting of the iron ore into steel, They
are even learning to do this. The picture is the first to

Royal Artillery, and Mrs ANGUS ROBERTS, whose husband is
in the King's Own Scottish Borderers, both work at the

te.text:
ONE OF THE OLDEST OF FARMING ARTS.              AW/RS

58-year-old Mr. Tom Allen Hancock, a smallholder at
Brook, Kent, is one of the few remaining exponents of
the thousands of years old art of flail-threshing.
The flail he uses was used by his father and his
grandfather before him and is nearly 150 years old.
It consists of a club swinging by a leather thong
from the end of a 5 ft pole; the pole is held in both
hands and the club swung to beat the sheaves of corn
laid out on the barn floor. Tom still relies on it
for threshing peas and beans.  He can remember the
days when his family had six men in the barn working
flails - keeping them occupied most of the winter.

Photo shows:-   Mr. Hancock threshing with his ancient
flail.

activity: the Green family, the first tenants of Poplar's first pre-fabricated hut homes, photographed around the fireside of their new home

te.text:
GREAVES.  D.H.  23rd. 10. 44.

Mr. and Mrs. John Green and their family are the
first to occupy a pre-fabricated hut house in Poplar.
10.000 of these hut homes are to be built in London.
Here are the Green family photographed round the
fireside of their new home in Glengall road, Poplar
tonight. L.-R. John, aged 7. Mrs. Green and
Christine, aged 3. Mr. Green. Margaret, aged 11. holding
Peter the family pet.
F192 / 3D HOUSING POST-WAR / EARLY POST WAR DIFFICULTIES / HOUSES/TEMPORARY PRE-FABS

AS the hands of the clock
pointed to six last night
three-year-old Christine
nodded in her chair before
the fire.
In a sleepy voice she said:
"Mummy, I want to go to my
cot."
These eight words told how
life has changed for Mr. and
Mrs. John Green and their
family of three.
Every night for the past five
months when Christine
wanted to go to bed, Mrs.
Green carried her out into
the garden from a bomb-
blasted kitchen to put her on
a bunk in a damp Anderson
shelter.
John, aged seven, and
Margaret, aged 11, followed
behind.
Mrs. Green went back to sleep
in a chair while her husband
slept on the floor. The back
kitchen was all the accommoda-
tion the fly-bombs had left them.
There was no room for them
to sit around the table for a
meal.
Yesterday the Green family
moved 200 yards down Glengall-
grove, Cubitt Town, Poplar, to
start a new life in a new home.
They are the first tenants of
Poplar's first hut-homes. Ten
thousand of them have been
promised as a temporary relief
for London's housing shortage.
It is not palatial; yet to Mrs.
Green it is a palace.
There are two bedrooms,
living-room and a partitioned-off
kitchenette.
Mrs. Green talked of the new
home.
"Think what it means to have
an electric cooker and to have
them all round the table for
proper meals; to have a nice
clean sink and good food cup-
boards and decent beds.
"I never gave up, and I always
managed to cook meals some-
how—but this is wonderful."

activity: pumping of 27,000 tons of oil from the tanker "British Skill" ashore to the Kent Oil Refinery on the Isle of Grain

te.text:
240963 DAW
FIRST OIL FOR ISLE OF GRAIN REFINERY.

Isle of Grain, Kent:  The pumping of 27,000 tons
of Kuwait oil from the tanker "British Skill"
today marked the initial operation towards
bringing "on stream" the first stage of the Anglo-
Iranian Oil Company's 40 million pound Kent Oil
Refinery on the Isle of Grain.
Work on the refinery began two and a half years
ago.  The distillation plant, which will be capable
of a throughput of four million tons of crude
oil annually, and its auxiliaries, as well as steam,
water and power services, are now almost ready
to go into operation.
PHOTO SHOWS:  The scene on the deck as the first
27,000 tons of oil is pumped ashore from the
British Skill.
In the background pipe lines lead away to the
giant refinery.
            31st. October, 1952   PN-d.

PLANET NEWS LTD
3, JOHNSON'S COURT,
LONDON, E.C. 4.
PHONE - CENT. 3671 & 3672/3

DAILY HERALD

activity: The exterior of a gasometer at Kennington Oval, specifically the rescue point where a boy had climbed the girders.

te.text:
By PETER BATT
A 13-YEAR-OLD boy clung to life by
his fingertips yesterday—130ft. high
on the famous Kennington Oval gaso-
meter.
Special constable John Laurance, aged 30,
inched his way along the topmost girder
and grasped the boy's hand. "Steady lad,"
he coaxed softly. "Hang on."
But the sobbing boy told him: "I'm tired.
I want to let go." And slumped unconscious.
The gasometer that loomed
over so many Test matches had
never known drama like this..
watched by hundreds in the
street below.
Hung on
For 30 nightmare minutes
Mr. Laurance hung on to the
boy's hand.
It slipped slowly from his
grasp, almost down to the finger-
tips. Then firemen reached
them.
They shouted to Mr. Laurance
to secure the boy to a girder by
tying a flagpole rope round him.
He then hung precariously,
clasping the boy's arm round a
girder as his other hand tied
the rope.
Firemen gently lowered the
boy in a bo'sun's chair. Mr.
Laurance climbed down a cat-
walk—and went home.
Said Thomas Spiers, a gas-
ometer workman: "Mr. Laur-
ance is the bravest man I've
ever seen. I couldn't have done
that for a million pounds."
Mr. Laurence, attached to
Bow-street police station, was
off duty when he saw the boy
hanging on high above.
Last night the police returned
the boy to an institution from
which he had escaped.
Rescue point—where the boy
clung to life.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
4 OCT 1962
PLEASE RETURN...

Youth Climbs
Gasometer at the Oval.

title: A photographic print of Industry, Fuel & Power - Coal, Accidents, Cambrian Colliery Rhondda, May 1965

date_info.rationale: Margin text date corresponds to the Cambrian Colliery disaster (May 17, 1965).

activity: Public gathering and official announcements following the Cambrian Colliery mining disaster.

te.text: Indus-Fuel & Power-Coal- Accidents- Cambrian Colliery, Rhonnda. May 1965

IN the Valley of Sorrow hundreds stood in silence last night to hear 31 names read out. This was the formal, official end to a day of tragedy.
Under sodium lights in Clydach Vale, the grim-faced Rhondda. The people gathered. The bereaved wives, mothers and children.
In the nearby Assembly Hall workmen who were still thinking: "It could have been us."
From a police car the loudspeaker drifted out, read by Glamorgan's Chief Constable, Mr. Melbourne
Last of all came the names of the dead rolled out, by the colliery manager, 42-year-old Ernest Breeze, and u n d e r - m a n a g e r Leslie Williams.
A GASP
A final gasp went up from the crowd. Mr. Thomas told them it would be as well if the list would be posted up for inspection.
"Perhaps he said, gently: "Then it would be as well to disperse to your homes." Reluctantly the people drifted home to ponder on the lovely little cul-de-sac of the Rhondda Valley.
In Clydach Vale today, the front doors are all open. Some women stand at their front gates, a few are still at the pithead.
There is no hope left—and no doubt.
All the dead miners have been identified by the numbers on their lamps. Nobody is unaccounted for.
The explosion was in the colliery's No. 1 pit — an up-to-date section of the colliery.
Thirty-one men in the immediate area of the blast were killed instantly.
WAS IT GAS?
How did it happen? It is possible gas seeped through from an old disused working at the weekend. An official inquiry will find the facts. The horror of it all. The Black Hell, as some miners called it—without trying to dramatise.
The victims were working 850ft. underground two and a half miles from the pit-head. They were in a tunnel only 2ft. 8in. high.
Rescue workers went down after the blast. But hope was never really there.
A worker who joined the rescue, his s h a k e n grey-faced, said: "The sight was terrible."
Some men were decapitated. Others without arms and legs. Their clothing was ripped to shreds.

activity: Rescue workers emerging from a pit shaft following a mine explosion.

te.text:
111 MEN TRAPPED IN PIT EXPLOSION
AT WHITEHAVEN CUMBERLAND. 16.8.47.
Six teams of rescue men and a 100 volunteer diggers
are this morning cutting through tons of fallen rock
in a fight to reach 71 miners stillentombed by an
explosion in the under-the-sea workings of the
William Pit, Whitehaven, Cumberland. At 2a.m. the rescue
squads had found 40 of the 111 men originally trapped.
All were dead, first news of the disaster came in an
emergancy call from the bottom of the pit shaft where
workers had felt the force of the explosion threeand a half
miles away , under the waters of the Solway Firth.
I.N.P. Two of the rescue workers coming up after
they had spent hours in trying to reach the
trapped men.
117/H/10277.
SPECIAL. INTERNATIONAL NEWS PHOTOS.

te.text:
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
- 6 SEP 1957
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY
Industries - Fuel and power - Oil - Refineries - British, misc

FOR FRIDAY'S DAILIES... SEPTEMBER 6

            A NEW TANKER JETTY FOR SCOTLAND      6.9.57

The first steel piles have been driven for a new tanker
jetty that is being built for British Petroleum Ltd. at
Finnart, on Loch Long, Scotland. When it is completed
in 1958, the jetty will accommodate the largest tankers.
The new jetty, which is about half a mile south of B.P.'s
present tanker jetty and installation, will have two concrete
decked shore arms each 180ft long. One arm will carry a
roadway for light vehicles and the other a pipe-track. The
jetty head, at which there will be a low water depth of
55 ft, will be 320 feet long.
Tankers will be able to         discharge up to 6,000 tons
an hour of crude oil         through two 24 inch pipelines
connecting with four new storage tanks now being built.
and the four tanks at the present installation. All these
tanks will be linked through the existing pumphouse
to the 57 miles pipeline to B.P.'s Grangemouth Refinery
on the Firth of Forth.
It was announced earlier this year that the annual
processing capacity of Grangemouth Refinery is to be
raised from 2,200,000 tons to 3,100,000 tons, This increased
capacity will be close to the annual carrying capacity
of the Finnart pipeline.
